POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Thu, 05 Nov 2026 21:23:43 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 EU targets large firms to unlock budget deal https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-targets-large-firms-to-unlock-budget-deal/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 05 Nov 2026 18:22:33 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9281160 European Council President António Costa suggested narrowing a controversial business tax to only apply to large firms with a turnover exceeding €750 million per year, two EU diplomats briefed on the discussions told POLITICO.

Costa hopes these concessions will facilitate an overall agreement on new EU-wide levies, known as own resources, which have emerged as a major stumbling bloc in the ongoing negotiations.

The idea was mentioned in meetings, known as “confessionals,” between Costa’s head of cabinet Pedro Lourtie and EU governments Thursday, to test the waters on the most sensitive aspects in the negotiations.

Lourtie overhauled an unpopular corporate tax known as CORE — which charges a lump sum on companies’ revenues exceeding €100 million — that the European Commission proposed last year.

According to his proposal, the EU would charge a 0.05% levy, as opposed to a lump sum. It would also only apply to firms with an annual turnover of more than €750 million.

These changes are expected to soften opposition among a group of countries led by Germany that challenged CORE on the grounds that it undermines competitiveness and takes a toll on medium-sized enterprises.

Going further

But two diplomats fear these concessions will not be enough to muster support for the new levy. “I don’t think this is going to solve the problem on CORE,” one told POLITICO. They, like others in this story, were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive negotiations.

France is pushing to introduce new taxes to reduce contributions to the EU budget.

In a concession to Paris, Costa’s team indicated that they won’t cut down on the total revenue projections from the Commission’s tax proposal from last year, which was expected to generate €65 billion annually. 

To generate additional resources for the budget, Costa’s team also suggested increasing two largely uncontroversial taxes on non-collected plastic and electronic waste that flows directly to the bloc’s budget by levying an additional 25 cents on each kilo.

The diplomats also proposed raising the share of a carbon imports’ tax that flows to the EU cash pot to 100% from the current 75%, and exploring levies on crypto firms and national spectrum auctions.

In a further concession, Lourtie suggested phasing in two taxes on tobacco products and polluting firms, known as the Emissions Trading System, for countries that are overwhelmingly affected.

Confessional diplomacy

The bilaterals, which started Thursday and will continue until next Monday, are expected to pave the way for a budget deal by the end of 2026 — before next year’s elections in Poland, France and Italy threaten to derail the negotiations.

Costa will put forward a new budget negotiating document on Nov. 21 ahead of a special summit the following week, said the two diplomats.

During Thursday’s meetings, Costa’s team signaled that the budget would be cut further, and reductions might affect regional funding known as cohesion policy.

That would be a major setback for an alliance of Southern and Eastern European countries, known as the Friends of Cohesion.

]]> en CBD edibles can’t be labeled organic, says EU court https://www.politico.eu/article/cbd-edibles-cant-be-labeled-organic-says-eu-court/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:53:32 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9280605 CBD edibles have become a popular supplement for relaxation — but that hasn’t stopped the EU’s top court from taking a high-strung approach to the bloc’s food rules.

The Court of Justice of the EU ruled Thursday that CBD-based food products cannot be certified as organic. The hangup: they’re not technically legal on the EU market.

It’s a bummer for consumers looking to grab some gummies with CBD derived without pesticides — and for the Professional Hemp Trade Association, which launched the case in France.  

CBD, or cannabidiol, is a non-psychoactive chemical component found in marijuana that’s gained a reputation as a way to take a chill pill without getting high. In some European countries, wellness shops are using a legal grey zone to sell CBD products that aren’t explicitly marketed for human consumption — often with a wink.   

In France, some hemp sellers wanted to sell them with an organic label. But the the judges shut that down. 

The European Commission classifies natural CBD as a so-called novel food, and it has yet to receive authorization to be sold on the EU market.  

The hemp sellers had challenged the refusal by France’s National Institute for Origin and Quality to grant organic certification to CBD edibles.  

The high court said that CBD can be certified as organic only after it is authorized for sale on the EU market.  

The certification is more than a decorative badge, the court reasoned, saying it “conveys a more general promise of quality and acceptance of a given product in the eyes of consumers, with this positive image being an intended commercial effect.” Putting it on a product that has not been approved for sale could be misleading. The Court’s ruling is also consistent with earlier national-level measures. 

The organic label setback looks to be the least of hemp sellers’ problems in France: Paris ordered edible CBD products to be pulled from the shelves completely this past May.

France’s digital minister Anne Le Hénanff told a French Senate hearing on Wednesday that she held two ministerial meetings in September and October to secure G7 commitments to a high-level working group to test frontier AI — the most advanced models — and share information about risks and incidents.

That effort “did not reach a successful conclusion” because the U.S. wanted to pursue its own approach, the French minister said.

“They are not prepared, at this stage, to issue a joint statement with the other six G7 nations, and have asked us to wait for the findings of their own assessment,” said Le Hénanff. “Naturally, we regret this, but we are continuing to move forward as Europeans on this issue.”

A White House official, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said that the French government proposed a “poorly defined body” to cooperate on AI that the administration feared would “create unnecessary bureaucracy.” 

The official pointed to U.S. President Donald Trump’s Super Intelligence Force, saying it brings government and industry together to accelerate innovation and ensure the safe deployment of models.

France, which holds the rotating presidency of the G7 for 2026, issued a chair’s summary statement after the Oct. 20 virtual G7 tech ministerial, which noted that ministers considered closer coordination on identifying risks and sharing incident information, as well as a dedicated high-level group. It was not a joint statement endorsed by all G7 members.

Le Hénanff has proposed resuming talks in December.

SI acceleration

Trump began promoting “super intelligence” as a replacement for “artificial intelligence” at the U.N. General Assembly in late September. A week later, he ordered federal agencies to use the new term.

G7 ministers in May agreed to discuss secure AI and risk assessment, which was followed by the G7 leaders meeting the following month in Évian.

But the stakes have risen as advanced AI systems gain unprecedented cyber capabilities that can be used for both attack and defense. In July, Hugging Face disclosed an intrusion driven by an autonomous AI agent. OpenAI later said models used in an internal cybersecurity test had bypassed controls and compromised parts of its own research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems.

Le Hénanff said France would keep pushing the issue, citing INESIA, France’s national AI evaluation and safety institute, and Inria, its public research institute for digital science and technology, as resources for the work.

]]> en Meloni urges ‘disorganized’ EU to speak with one voice on Ukraine https://www.politico.eu/article/giorgia-meloni-urges-eu-unity-ukraine/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 05 Nov 2026 14:20:56 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9279375 ROME — The EU is giving the impression of being “all over the place” when it comes to Ukraine, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told European Council President António Costa.

In a letter seen by POLITICO, Meloni said that discussing how the EU can speak with one voice on Ukraine should be added to the agenda of an informal leaders’ meeting in Dublin next week, adding that the issue “can no longer be postponed.”

Meloni pointed out the various formats that have been used to discuss Ukraine, including meetings in Miami and Oslo, and upcoming talks scheduled by the Coalition of the Willing and the European Political Community, plus the phone call that Finland’s Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre made to Russia’s Vladimir Putin. She said the multiple forums were “undermining our credibility in handling one of the most complicated issues our nations are facing.”

While the EU has repeatedly insisted it gets a “seat at the table” at Ukraine peace talks, to safeguard the region’s interests and bolster Kyiv’s ability to resist a lopsided deal, the bloc has yet to agree on a single leader or institution to spearhead negotiations.

“I’m convinced that we all realize how, by projecting the image of a Europe that’s all over the place, we’re doing nothing but serving the interests of those who want this war to continue,” the Italian prime minister wrote. “And I think this is unacceptable, given that human lives and the future of our security are at stake.”

“Proceeding in a disorganized manner, with initiatives that chase one another and overlap, will not help us — neither with our partners nor with those we must convince to stop this senseless aggression,” she added.

“I am not asking for a seat for Italy in this or that format,” she said.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told POLITICO he agrees with Meloni. “We need to have a legitimate representation of Europe in the process because we pay for this war.” 

Eastern Europe and Scandinavia also need to be part of the conversation, he said, adding his preferred format would be to stick to Treaty of Lisbon — which laid out a unified foreign policy — plus possibly the U.K.

Writing in response to Meloni on Thursday evening, Costa thanked the Italian premier for setting out her concerns “so clearly” and said he agreed “Europe needs to act with coherence, unity and determination.”

“The European Union’s participation must be organised in a manner that enables it to convey a clear and unified message,” he wrote. “Indeed, the European Union’s interests need to be represented by its institutions, in accordance with the Treaties. As you know, I have raised this issue on several previous occasions in our discussions between Leaders.”

EU leaders meet in Dublin for an informal European Council on Nov. 13. A meeting of the European Political Community, which involves all EU states plus Ukraine and other allies, takes place the day before.

As the format for talks increasingly coalesces around the E3 — the U.K., France and Germany — alongside the EU, NATO and Ukraine, Italy has found itself sidelined.

Rome was excluded from meetings in Miami in October and Brussels this week, although it did take part in talks in Oslo at the invitation of the Norwegian government. An Italian national security adviser attended a working dinner there, but Italy’s participation came in place of France, rather than as an additional seat at the table.

Over the past year, Italy has emerged as the EU’s most vocal and persistent advocate for appointing a special envoy for Russia-Ukraine peace talks. Meloni first publicly floated the proposal in January, arguing that the bloc needed to “speak with one voice” and engage directly with Moscow.

While other countries, including France, Austria, Czechia and Luxembourg, have also expressed support for the idea, Rome has led the push, with Italian officials repeatedly raising it on the sidelines of EU summits and in discussions among EU ambassadors preparing leaders’ meetings.

Ahead of the latest EU summit in October, Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani seized an opportunity during an exchange with reporters at a European People’s Party pre-summit gathering to renew the call for a special envoy.

Asked whether Costa himself should take on the role, Tajani praised him but insisted that the priority was for Europe to have “a spokesperson who can negotiate” and articulate a “univocal position,” warning that otherwise EU foreign policy would appear weak.

Nick Vinocur, Gerardo Fortuna, Zoya Sheftalovich and Elena Giordano contributed reporting. This article has been updated with a response from António Costa.

]]> en Mélenchon’s mission for his young fans: Debate boomers on Facebook https://www.politico.eu/article/france-jean-luc-melenchon-mission-for-his-young-fans-debate-boomers-on-facebook/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 05 Nov 2026 14:08:20 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9269016 PARIS — Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s campaign has a plan for winning over older French voters: get his young supporters to sign up for Facebook to talk to their parents.

Mélenchon, 75, may be the oldest candidate in next spring’s race to replace Emmanuel Macron. But his progressive platform and call for a civic revolution have made him a hit with younger voters, who are more likely to scroll through TikTok and Snapchat than through the old-school social network.

“We’re strong [on every other social media platform],” said Antoine Léaument, who handles the Mélenchon campaign’s communication operations. “Facebook is one of the places where the digital battle could be decisive.”

More than 40% of voters younger than 35 plan to vote for Mélenchon, according to a recent Cluster17 poll commissioned by POLITICO. That figure drops to 14% or less across the age brackets over 50 — groups that, if they use social media at all, tend to favor Facebook over its newer rivals.

According to Médiamétrie, France’s leading audience measurement company, platforms like Instagram and Snapchat have 35% more daily users than Facebook among 15-to-24-year-olds.

On TikTok, which skews younger, Mélenchon has about twice the following of any other presidential candidate.

“Their digital campaign is paying off very quickly,” said a strategist from a competing campaign, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. The strategist also underlined that the share of comments on social media posts describing Mélenchon in a positive light was rapidly rising despite how he’s been vilified by his opponents.

But on Facebook, Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally reigns.

Since June, National Rally posts have drawn more than 2 million reactions, more than those of any other French political party, according to data from social monitoring platform Visibrain shared with POLITICO. The page of the National Rally’s local branch in the small region of Vienne alone generated more reactions than the pages of Macron’s Renaissance party.

“Engagement on Facebook is very concentrated,” around the National Rally, Visibrain said.

Listen to the kids

Recent polls show that Mélenchon’s core base of young voters puts him in a strong position to secure a second-place finish in the first round of the presidential election. That would earn him a spot in a runoff against Le Pen, who has held a double-digit lead for first place in surveys for months. (French presidential elections advance to a two-candidate second round if no one wins 50% of the vote on the first try.)

Beating Le Pen, however, will require winning over larger swaths of the electorate. Though pollsters and political scientists urge caution about polling a runoff so early in a campaign, the second-round surveys pitting Le Pen against Mélenchon show the far-left candidate on track for a crushing defeat.

Many older voters remain undecided about what they would do when faced with that match-up, so the answer could lie in whether they decide to listen to their children.

Léaument has been rallying activists from Mélenchon’s France Unbowed to share content en masse on the platform via an open WhatsApp channel, which currently counts over 170,000 members, posting calls to action or campaign clips to share on their social media accounts.

“WE MUST RE-ENGAGE WITH FACEBOOK AT ALL COSTS! WE MUST NOT LEAVE ANY GROUND TO THE FAR RIGHT,” he urged activists in a message posted to the channel.

That playbook is partly borrowed from André Janones, the Brazilian lawmaker who used the messaging app to mobilize supporters of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of his surprise reelection last month.

It has at least one obvious limitation: Political parties have no control over social media algorithms. In Brazil, Lula’s campaign alleged that Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, was boosting Bolsonaro and suppressing its content — an allegation Meta denied.

Hadrien Clouet, a France Unbowed MP who closely tracks South American politics, said lessons would need to be drawn on how the Mélenchon campaign can “protect [itself] from the influence of U.S. social networks.”

But the underlying idea of having the young convince — if not pressure — their elders has been pushed by the movement’s leadership for several months already.

At a party event over the summer, Mathilde Panot, France Unbowed’s top lawmaker in parliament, invoked the work of French political scientist Vincent Tiberj, who has studied “inverse socialization,” or how children challenge and sometimes change their parents’ views and politics.

She pointed to the 2024 vote to make abortion a constitutional right in France, saying that several lawmakers were pressured into voting in favor of the proposal by their daughters — a point French media also reported at the time.

“The children need to convince their parents,” Panot said. “We need to do some grassroots work, to go out and convince people one by one, and that starts with our inner circle: parents, brothers and sisters, uncles and aunts.”

]]> en How NATO can turn data into defense advantage https://www.politico.eu/sponsored-content/how-nato-can-turn-data-into-defense-advantage/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 05 Nov 2026 13:36:20 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=sponsored-content&p=9278271 Data is redefining modern defense operations. The ability to master and manage it is now a decisive factor in military victory or defeat. Few people know that better than Jean Charles Ellermann-Kingombe, assistant secretary general for cyber and digital transformation at NATO.

In a recent interview preceding NATO Edge 26, the Alliance’s annual defense innovation show, Ellermann-Kingombe is very clear on the kind of digital transformation effort it takes to get the right data into the hands of military leaders operating in high-pressure situations, at exactly the time and place they need it.

Data-sharing must be a core design principle, he says: “The bottleneck is often not technology, but permission: classification boundaries, national rules and trust decisions.” Once data is well managed, an even bigger opportunity arises to use AI as “an enabler of military effectiveness,” he says, assisting commanders and operators further.

He adds: “For NATO, the biggest difference AI can make is in decision advantage. Modern operations generate volumes of data that no human organisation can process unaided at the speed required. AI can help fuse information, detect patterns, support planning, prioritise scarce resources and accelerate staff processes, providing commanders with better insight, earlier warnings and more resilient options.”

As powerful as it is, AI can only reliably accelerate defense mission outcomes if it is built on vast, relevant and quality data. Data is the fuel that will power the shift to software-defined defense, an approach that delivers military capability through flexible, modular software rather than rigid, hardware-bound platforms.

THE CHALLENGES OF MASTERING DATA

Software-defined defense, AI and the challenge of mastering the data that powers both, will be hot topics for attendees at NATO Edge 26, due to be held in Izmir, Türkiye, in November and expected to attract over 3,000 participants and more than 270 technology partners, including Elastic.

We will be there because we know that many attendees will be looking to better understand what software-defined defense will demand of them in data management terms.

As powerful as it is, AI can only reliably accelerate defense mission outcomes if it is built on vast, relevant and quality data. Data is the fuel that will power the shift to software-defined defense.

Bringing data together from many intelligent systems and smart devices demands real rigor. After all, in order to make critical operational decisions, military personnel need to be able to see the big picture, quickly searching for information in both structured and unstructured data formats across a vast array of different systems.

Defense data naturally lives wherever operations happen — across land, sea, air, space and cyber domains — and is stored in different formats like images, audio transcripts, documents and geospatial, reaching across thousands of different mission systems.

These can include communications systems that keep troops connected in the field; systems used to manage artillery devices; reconnaissance systems; radar stations; and geographical information systems that support military leaders in tracking assets, planning missions and routes, and analyzing risks and threats, including potential ambush sites and minefields.

In order to make critical operational decisions, military personnel need to be able to see the big picture, quickly searching for information in both structured and unstructured data formats across a vast array of different systems.

On top of all this, organizations like NATO face an additional layer of complexity. Building a common operational picture across the digital environments of 32 member nations requires multi-intelligence fusion of massive volumes of data held in disparate systems, from legacy databases and classified networks to cloud platforms and security tools.

OPERATIONAL ADVANTAGE

Addressing these challenges means turning all this data into operational advantage and mission readiness, accelerating the ability of armed forces to respond to situations by increasing their situational awareness and decision speed.

The answer is a data mesh architecture. Rather than consolidating everything into a traditional data lake, a data mesh approach manages data where it originates and lives, without moving or duplicating it; so it can be searched, queried and analyzed from multiple access points across the entire environment, including allied partners such as NATO member nations. That is what turns scattered data into one unified operational picture with near real-time insights, and context, giving commanders the situational awareness and decision speed that mission-readiness depends on. In my view, it is the most flexible and scalable way to get there.

It also speaks directly to the permission bottleneck Ellermann-Kingombe describes. Because data stays under the control of the nation or system that owns it, access can be governed by policy at the source, with classification boundaries and national rules enforced where the data lives rather than negotiated away in a central repository.

Rather than consolidating everything into a traditional data lake, a data mesh approach manages data where it originates and lives, without moving or duplicating it.

A data mesh approach is sustainable because of its reliance on open standards. They enable defense organizations to connect systems that were never designed to work together, from legacy platforms to dispersed infrastructure, so data stays findable and can be effectively analyzed across the environment. Interoperability stops being a barrier as new partners and data sources join, and new tools can be integrated without rebuilding systems or making major investments. The architecture scales alongside the Alliance’s growth.

Without a unified view, the risk of losing operational advantage to adversaries extends from the battlefield into cyberspace. Zero Trust depends on connecting authentication logs, network traffic and application telemetry where they already sit, so that traditionally separate domains can be visualized and analyzed together. When a user accesses sensitive data, the system must verify not only who they are but also their device status, network path, and the time and location of access. If those checks are slow or impossible, threats can remain undetected and escalate through systems. A data mesh built on open standards connects the pillars of a Zero Trust architecture, allowing organizations to accelerate implementation without replacing the tools they already have.

When the manual efforts of military data analysts struggle to keep pace with the scale and speed of events on the ground, AI can work faster and more accurately.

The same logic is already visible in large government organizations: CISA’s new SIEM-as-a-Service platform uses open standards to give US federal civilian agencies a consistent approach to threat detection and response.

As AI’s value in supporting human decision-making becomes increasingly clear, a data mesh architecture provides the foundation to apply agentic AI capabilities holistically. It enables complex organizations to analyze the vast amounts of data their systems generate, find actionable correlations and separate signals from noise. When the manual efforts of military data analysts struggle to keep pace with the scale and speed of events on the ground, AI can work faster and more accurately. It also lets analysts ask questions across structured and unstructured data and rapidly receive answers grounded in reliable sources.

The numerous tech challenges facing the modern military calls for closer NATO-industry cooperation, and that’s why NATO Edge 26 is such an important event. All 32 sovereign member states that make up the Alliance use different systems, yet they rely on secure, trusted data-sharing with each other as the foundation for cooperating on military operations and sharing intelligence. It’s vital that they can turn to industry innovators to support their operational needs.

At a time of great geopolitical uncertainty, with data increasingly considered a primary defense asset, NATO members face growing pressure to turn it into operational advantage and readiness before adversaries do. We look forward to discussing how at NATO Edge 26.

]]> en Burnham won’t follow Trump in actively inviting Putin to G20 https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-burnham-donald-trump-invite-vladimir-putin-g20/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 05 Nov 2026 13:32:21 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9278982 LONDON — Vladimir Putin won’t be at the G20 summit in the U.K. next year, Andy Burnham said in an interview published Thursday.

Pushed by the Economist magazine on whether the Russian president will be invited to the gathering of world leaders in Manchester next November, the British PM said: “No.”

He went on to clarify the guest list is “handled by the G20,” but stressed Russia would not be present “because of an outstanding sanction.”

Burnham’s decision to actively exclude Putin comes after U.S. President Donald Trump sparked a diplomatic row by inviting the Russian leader to America’s G20 summit in Miami this December.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband previously told POLITICO Britain will not ditch its ban on directly engaging with Russia, but that it was for the U.S. to make its own decisions.

A photocall at the G20 foreign ministers meeting last week was canceled after politicians, including Miliband, refused to be pictured with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

The U.K. has been one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters since Russia’s full-scale invasion of the country in 2022 — a policy followed by all the five British prime ministers in post during nearly five years of war.

Burnham also told the Economist he’s keen to host Xi Jinping after the Chinese president visited Manchester in 2015, and said there’s a “real opportunity” for future U.K.-China economic collaboration after his predecessor Keir Starmer’s visit to Beijing earlier this year.

This story has been updated to reflect a full transcript of Burnham’s interview with The Economist.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 05 Nov 2026 17:17:54 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Internal energy papers show “half-hearted” EU commission efforts to save methane rules https://euobserver.com/247205/leaked-energy-papers-show-half-hearted-eu-commission-efforts-to-save-methane-rules/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247205 As ambassadors meet again to decide how long to delay the EU’s methane rules, internal documents show how the commission did too little to save them.]]> For the third time in a matter of weeks, EU ambassadors will try on Friday (6 November) to agree whether to delay the EU’s methane rules for oil and gas imports by one year or by three.

Big Oil, the Trump administration and a growing group of member states have been pushing for a delay, citing supply and legal risks.

For a long time the commission refused to propose a delay, but in October it finally buckled and proposed one year.

Much of what led up to that has been reported, including on our pages. But we obtained 55 internal documents from the commission’s energy department that show how it tried to handle the pressure, and eventually failed.

They cover more than a year, from the first talks with the Trump administration in March 2025 to the spring of 2026.

US dislike of the rules has not been a secret. Trump officials and allied industry groups attacked the EU methane regulation openly and regularly. 

Climate wise there is a lot at stake. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas that traps around 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide over 20 years. A lot of it leaks into the atmosphere from wells, pipelines and gas terminals.

]]> Listen: Drug trafficking is ramping in Europe, why and what are the consequences ?  https://euobserver.com/247225/listen-drug-trafficking-is-ramping-in-europe-why-and-what-are-the-consequences/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:09:27 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247225 The trial of 5 men suspected of brutal killings associated with France’s major drug cartel should come to an end in Aix-en Provence this Friday (6th of November).]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

The trial of 5 men suspected of brutal killings associated with France’s major drug cartel should come to an end in Aix-en Provence this Friday (6th of November).

France has been particularly affected by the ramp up of drug trafficking and related violences across Europe in recent years. But how has drug trafficking transformed into one of the major threats to European security? And what solutions are put forward in Europe?

While during the 60s-70s, European port cities like Marseille were transit zones for drugs directed to the North American market, Europe is now a key consumer market for production, which is exploding too.

Western and Central Europe is currently the second largest cocaine market in the world according to the UN’s office on drugs and crime. And levels of use are clearly increasing since 2015. 

When it comes to Eastern Europe, it has the highest prevalence of people who inject drugs worldwide : 1.3 percent in 2024.

In parallel, the quantity of drugs seized in the EU between 2014 and 2024 has surged dramatically: the amount of seized methamphetamine multiplied by 11, and five times more cocaine. 

Read more

From the Netherlands to Sierra Leone: EU aid, a president’s daughter and Europe’s most‑wanted cocaine boss

A recent investigation by the Guardian directly links the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe with the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe and the close ties they’ve forged with local mafias.

This intensification of drug trafficking in Europe, has been accompanied by a surge in correlated violences. The 2023 Eurojust report signalled that half of all homicides recorded in Europe were directly connected to drug trafficking.

Here in Brussels, 74 shootings were recorded  between January and September 2026, resulting in two deaths and 28 injuries. 

So what should we do about it ?

Last month, the European Parliament voted a resolution demanding a coordinated EU crackdown on drug trafficking networks. The resolution demands more funding on police equipment, tighter security at ports and a deepening of collaboration between customs, law enforcement and judicial authorities across the bloc.

But while nationally, right and far-right politicians call for harsher punitive approaches – other voices call for alternative solutions.

Read more

Brussels’ drug war in Saint-Gilles: residents caught between bombs, shootings and an absent state

One of these voices is anti-mafia French activist Amine Kessaci. The Marseille-born 23 year old is the brother of one of the victims of the 3 killings currently on trial. Recruited by a drug gang as a teenager, his brother Brahim was shot and burned in a car in 2020.

Now part of the French Green party, Kessaci argues that drug gangs “fill a void” left by a lack of public services, offering an illusion of economic opportunities to teenagers from economically precarious families, who feel abandoned by the school system and entrapped in the margins of society.

Similarly, Belgium’s national commissary to drugs Ine Van Wymersch underlines that the one third of young Brusselers living under the poverty line, are particularly vulnerable to criminal organisations which consider them as an “easy-to-recruit” and “disposable” workforce.

Van Wymersch warns against the counter-productive effects of repressive approaches and calls to “transform the living environment of vulnerable youth” by supporting parents, offering better access to public neighbourhood structures and creating better adapted work experience opportunities.

Van Wymersch’s recommendations also include the creation of a “Child File” from birth to detect risk factors such as poverty, family histories of crime, and low levels of education. ]]> Chinese spy suspect walks free after Prague court acquittal, while Czech spy suspect in China remains behind bars https://euobserver.com/246959/chinese-spy-suspect-walks-free-after-prague-court-acquittal-while-czech-spy-suspect-in-china-remains-behind-bars/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:01:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246959 Yang Yiming, a suspected Chinese spy, has walked free after a Czech court acquitted him, but prosecutors have appealed the verdict. However, Czech national Aleš K. is still behind bars in China for allegedly breaching the country's security laws.]]> First published in Respekt.

Yang Yiming, a suspected Chinese spy, has walked free after his arrest earlier this year in the Czech Republic.

Prague Municipal Court judge Tome Frankič found that Yiming posed as a foreign correspondent for a Chinese media outlet while working for the country’s intelligence services. He accepted assignments to covertly pass on information he obtained about politicians and other public figures.

And yet, the man was released this week on Monday (2 November). In the view of judge Frankič, the evidence against Yiming did not show he broke the law.

Read more

Czech businessman detained by Beijing faces espionage charges and could be part of swap with Chinese spy

Suspected Chinese spy walks free

In court, the prosecution failed to prove Yiming had “intentionally endangered or damaged the constitutional order, territorial integrity, defence or security of the Czech Republic, or undermined its sovereignty.”

The trial of the Chinese man was the first of its kind in modern-day Czech Republic.

Previously, espionage could be prosecuted only if police or intelligence services could prove that a person had obtained classified information such as government documents or intelligence-service materials.

But the Czech security community argued for years that defining the offence of spying was defined too narrowly, and could not adequately tackle espionage.

Indeed, collecting information on people’s private lives – whether it be their alcoholism or intimate relationships – could be enough to blackmail some to advance the interests of foreign powers.

So the previous Czech government passed a new, broader criminal offence – unauthorised activity for a foreign power.

Now, bringing someone before a Czech court requires proof of activities for a foreign power with intent to endanger the Czech Republic’s constitutional order, sovereignty, territorial integrity, defence or security.

]]> Chief trade MEP Bernd Lange slams EU Commission for ‘hiding’ behind voting rules on banning Israeli settlement imports https://euobserver.com/247198/bernd-lange-slams-eu-commission-for-hiding-behind-voting-rules-on-banning-israeli-settlement-imports/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 15:45:38 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247198 MEPs scolded the EU Commission for failing to propose legislation on banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements.]]> Senior European Commission officials have been scolded by MEPs for their refusal to propose a trade ban on illegal Israeli settlements.

The EU could ban the trade with a qualified majority vote among EU states, according lawyers at the council, representing member states. But the commission favours a controversial unanimity vote.

Read more

Most EU countries back ‘full ban’ on Israeli settler imports — but unanimity fight looms

Léon Delvaux, a European Commission official, said no decision on which option or combination of options has been taken.

“So far, no majority has come about on any of these options,” he said on Thursday (5 November) at a meeting in European Parliament’s trade committee.

“With incompatible positions, it has not been possible to find a way forward that satisfies the different viewpoints,” added Vladimir Janecek from the EU’s foreign policy branch, the European External Action Service (EEAS).

But that logic drew ire among MEPs who point out that the commission regularly proposes legislation without first seeking majority support among EU states.

“It’s totally unacceptable,” said Bernd Lange, a German Socialists & Democrats MEP who chairs the trade committee.

“It’s totally new for me that you are asking before presenting legislation, the council has a qualified majority. It’s crazy,” he said.

]]> MEPs at odds with the public as poll shows huge majority against loosening pesticide rules https://euobserver.com/247138/meps-at-odds-with-the-public-as-poll-shows-huge-majority-against-loosening-pesticide-rules/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 15:25:39 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247138 Between 68-80 percent of Europeans across seven EU states want to phase-out rather than increase pesticide use, according to a new poll. But MEPs appear determined to go in the other direction.]]> An overwhelming majority of Europeans oppose plans by EU lawmakers to weaken the regulation of pesticides or expand their use further, according to a new survey published on Thursday (5 November). 

A YouGov poll of more than 7,000 people across France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Romania and Spain found that support for unlimited pesticide approval stands at between four to six percent in France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland and Spain, and 10 percent in Romania. The poll was commissioned by Pan Europe, an environmental lobby group.

Meanwhile, hefty majorities of between 68 percent (in Spain) and 80 percent in Romania say that pesticides should be phased out completely. The survey also found that opposition to increased pesticide use prevails across the political spectrum, with conservative and centre-right voters only marginally more in favour of deregulation on pesticides than greens and leftists. 

However, the survey findings are at odds with the direction of the “Food and Feed Safety” proposal tabled by the EU Commission last December and, in particular, of leading MEPs who want to deregulate more than the commission. 

The commission proposal would make unlimited approvals for pesticide active substances the norm, scrapping the regular safety reviews that have allowed 54 harmful substances to be banned since the EU pesticide regulation entered into force in 2011. 

Under the existing rules, pesticides are approved for a limited period and must be reassessed every 10 to 15 years. 

“The message is clear: unlimited pesticide approvals have no public support, not even from conservative and far-right voters. MEPs pushing to weaken pesticide safeguards are out of step with the people they represent”, said Salomé Roynel, policy officer at PAN Europe.

]]> Details emerge of Russian atrocity: dropping three-tonne bombs on civilians at food bank and shelter (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,715) https://euobserver.com/247163/details-emerge-of-russian-atrocity-dropping-three-tonne-bombs-on-civilians-at-food-bank-and-shelter-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1715/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 14:21:55 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247163 Newly released police body-camera footage and analysis by independent Russian investigators puncture Moscow’s claims they hit a “military target”, exposing how rescue workers and civilians were lured into a shelter in Komyshuvakha before being annihilated. ]]>
  • Harrowing footage from a police body camera shows that Russians were attacking civilians in Komyshuvakha.
  • Monday’s attack is the deadliest in terms of casualties since at least 2023.
  • What Russian propaganda says about the war crime — and why independent Russian analysts also dismiss it as lies.
  • October figures on frontline shifts according to Finland’s Black Bird Group: Russians barely moved.
  • Charts of the day: Russia lost more aircraft than tanks in October.
  • Videos of the day: FPV drones hang from wires like birds; the difficult journey of Russian logistics.

    • The largest attack on civilians in at least the past two years. World media have focused on the US elections in recent days, and so it has somewhat gone unnoticed that Russia committed one of the largest attacks on civilians in Ukraine since the start of the war.

    It happened on Monday morning in the village of Komyshuvakha in Zaporizhzhia oblast, around 15 km from the front line.

    Source: DeepState UA

    On Monday morning, Russians attacked the school complex, where humanitarian aid was being distributed to local residents.

    In total, they dropped at least nine glide bombs, some of them weighing three tonnes. Such a bomb weighs roughly twice as much as a Škoda Octavia car and contains up to 1.4 tonnes of explosives. Russia primarily uses these bombs to destroy underground bunkers.

    This time, however, they did not hit Ukrainian soldiers but civilians.

    What happened: By Thursday morning, it was known that at least 42 people had been killed in the attack on Komyshuvakha. This alone makes it the worst attack on civilians in Ukraine since 2023.

    A further 33 people remained missing, apparently buried beneath the rubble. It is therefore quite possible that the total death toll will rise significantly, making this the worst attack on civilians since the bombing of the theatre bearing the word “Children” in Mariupol in 2022.

    It is one of the worst things Russia has done during the war. Russian propaganda, however, has sought to portray the attack differently. It claims that the site of the attack was a base for Ukrainian soldiers or police officers.

    On Wednesday, Ukrainians released harrowing footage recorded by a camera attached to a police officer’s body. It suggests that the Russians knew full well whom they were attacking.

    ]]>         ‘Emotional part’ of Polish court crisis is ‘closer to over’ says Tusk, amid talks of EU mediation https://euobserver.com/247055/polish-government-is-open-to-eu-mediation-on-court-crisis-justice-minister-says/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 13:53:28 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247055 The "very emotional part" of a conflict between the government and right-wing Polish president Karol Nawrocki over the appointment of judges and ambassadors is almost over, according to prime minister Donald Tusk.]]> The “very emotional part” of a conflict between the government and right-wing Polish president Karol Nawrocki over the appointment of judges and ambassadors is almost over, according to prime minister Donald Tusk.

    “From my point of view the legal problem is solved,” Tusk told reporters on Thursday (5 November).

    “If I talk with the president [Nawrocki] I will try to convince him that it is in our common interest to reduce, or at least to have emotions under full control, when it comes to the situation of the Constitutional Court,” he added.

    Earlier, justice minister Waldemar Żurek told reporters that the government would be open to EU mediation to resolve the dispute, but that Brussels had not yet offered such talks and Warsaw had not yet requested them. 

    “We are open to mediation … but it takes two to tango,” Żurek also told a group of reporters at the chancellery of the prime minister in Warsaw.

    “You need to have a partner to talk to before you reach consensus,” he added.

    His remarks come after a confrontation over the composition of Poland’s highest court arose after Nawrocki refused to accept the oaths of judges elected by parliament’s centre-right majority.

    His decision prompted a senior judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, to assume leadership of the Constitutional Tribunal, in a move that has sparked days-long protests in front of the court building by the right-wing opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS) and its supporters.

    Officials in Warsaw say that 46 ambassador appointments are also waiting to be signed off by the president.

    Tusk wants to “stabilise” the situation and will be holding talks with president Nawrocki, Żurek told reporters, falling short on the details of such talks.

    “Will there be a breakthrough? We cannot tell the judges that were elected legally [by parliament] to go home,” he also said.

    Read more

    [Explainer] Polish right turns court dispute into election battleground, dragging in the EU

    Attempts to politicise the court started in 2015 under the previous authoritarian government, led by PiS, which was in office until 2023. 

    Żurek described the Constitutional Tribunal as “the last fortress” for PiS, which had decided that the court was “their property”, he said. 

    The prosecutor’s office was also starting to take action against Bogdan Święczkowski, the tribunal’s PiS-aligned official head, who was facing embezzlement charges, and PiS was “afraid” that “their people will face the courts”,  Żurek added.

    Święczkowski, who used to be a chief prosecutor under PiS’s former justice minister, has also been charged with using spyware to target a solicitor in a politically charged case.

    Material recorded using the spyware system could include private talks with Tusk, the solicitor’s client at the time, or discussions of a legal case against PiS’s chairman, Jarosław Kaczyński.

    ]]>         Europe should beware of buying America’s increasingly unaccountable AI killing-machines https://euobserver.com/246875/europe-should-beware-of-buying-americas-increasingly-unaccountable-ai-killing-machines/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:13:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246875 As Washington hands its autonomous warfare roadmap to Musk and other defence-industry moguls, European leaders in Geneva must decide whether to copy a model that speeds up killing, while hollowing out accountability for civilian deaths.]]> Later this month in Geneva, states will gather for the Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons and decide whether to begin negotiating binding rules on autonomous weapons.

    More than 70 states have already indicated their readiness to do so. Meanwhile, Washington is moving in the opposite direction.

    The gap between Washington and its allies on autonomous weapons has direct implications for how responsibility is built into military technology. 

    On 30 September, the US department of war announced an Autonomous Warfare Command, meant to scale autonomous warfare across the US military by October 2027.

    The same speech launched Project Meridian, a 120-day study of the technologies the US military will need for future wars. The project will be led by tech oligarch Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey (CEO of defence firm Anduril), and US politician Newt Gingrich, with the group’s findings due in January. 

    Ethical and commercial issues abound. SpaceX is a backbone of US national security, and Anduril sells jammers, interceptors, and un-crewed combat aircraft to the US military.

    Critics have noted that Musk and Luckey would be identifying needs that their own companies already meet, and the announcement describes no recusal or disclosure mechanism.

    Others, such as professor Elke Schwarz from the. Queen Mary University of London, have long shown how the commercial logic of technology firms shapes the ethics of violent technologies, treating moral and legal questions as engineering problems to be optimised away.

    Read more

    Russia’s faith in ‘error-free’ killer robots and global divisions expose the moral vacuum in AI warfare

    From a technical and legal perspective, this is neither possible nor desirable. Project Meridian promises that this logic will set the agenda. 

    What this agenda fails to cover is just as consequential. The US administration of president Donald Trump has dismantled the machinery that teaches militaries about civilian harm.

    The Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence fell from 40 staff to nine in 2025, and the Pentagon’s own inspector general concluded the department no longer has the personnel and capabilities needed to meet its legal responsibilities.

    Organisations like Airwars, which document civilian harm from military operations, find themselves offering evidence to commands that have almost no one left to receive it, let alone learn lessons to improve practices over time. 

    Autonomy and AI-enabled targeting depend on high quality data and feedback. A system is only as good as what its operators learn from its errors.

    Research on the quantification logics of targeting, and on outdated intelligence feeding strike decisions, shows how easily speed and scale displace the judgment that precautions require.

    Accelerating autonomy while abandoning the ability to learn from past practices does not produce a more precise or legitimate military.

    It produces a faster one that repeats its mistakes, which will continue to exacerbate civilian harm in new theatres of war. 

    Read more

    First fully-autonomous drone kill Ukraine heralds ‘dystopian future of untethered weaponry’

    Washington exporting normalisation

    This issue is relevant to discussions in Geneva because technology that is built, bought and normalised in Washington is sold elsewhere.

    European militaries integrate, procure and operate alongside American systems.

    And the diplomatic track is losing ground on exactly this point: the Group of Governmental Experts’ final report softened what earlier drafts framed as obligations on responsibility and accountability into encouragement. 

    This moment also offers opportunities. Europe is in a position to answer with more than just words.

    Responsibility works best when it is designed into a system from the start.

    Read more

    Why Pope Leo is right to call on EU to regulate lethal AI weapons

    Precautions must be built in at the design stage, with deliberate friction where speed would erode judgment, meaningful human decision-making, and sustained engagement among developers, lawyers, and operators.

    States already have duties to review new weapons and to protect civilians. Applying these across the whole lifecycle of a system takes institutional will, and Europe is uniquely positioned to demonstrate this. 

    This will also strengthen European sovereignty. Relying on a handful of American vendors means importing their design assumptions along with their products.

    European standards for testing and assurance, limiting civilian harm written into procurement contracts, and legal review that begins at the design stage would give governments real choices about what they buy and on what terms.

    Any supplier, American or European, would have to meet them. 

    In Geneva, European governments should back the start of negotiations on a legal instrument, and they should write responsibility by design into their own procurement now, without waiting for a treaty.

    Europe should demand a different theory of responsibility from whoever supplies its autonomy.

    The crisis began in December 2015, when Poland’s then-governing Law and Justice party (PiS) appointed three judges to seats that had already been filled.

    What followed was a sustained effort to bring the country’s constitutional watchdog under political control.     This constitutes a breach of – not a defence – of the rule of law. Yet the president’s obstruction does not give the government unlimited discretion in how it restores the tribunal. Its response must also comply with the law.

    ]]>         Is the Western Sahara now friendless? No, EU backing for Morocco is conditional, and Spanish election will be pivotal https://euobserver.com/246595/is-the-western-sahara-now-friendless-no-eu-backing-for-morocco-is-conditional-and-spanish-election-will-be-pivotal/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246595 Spain's general election could be, in part, a referendum on the country's partnership with Morocco, with the opposition promising tougher border control measures and closer ties with Rabat's neighbour and enemy, Algeria.]]> The collapse of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a 35 year mandate, is the latest diplomatic win for Morocco, but Rabat’s European support may prove to be less conclusive than it thinks. 

    The end came at a UN Security Council last week, when the United States and Russia effectively cancelled each other out by vetoing rival resolutions on extending the mandate of the UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara. 

    Russia vetoed a US-drafted resolution on Western Sahara at the Security Council on Friday (30 October), leaving the UN peacekeeping mission without a renewed mandate just a day before it expired. 

    The US resolution would have extended the mission for another year but enshrining a plan to give Western Sahara limited autonomy under Morocco’s sovereignty as the only basis ‌for talks to settle the dispute that dates back to the end of Spanish colonialism in the 1970s. The US text also proposed to remove any reference to a referendum among the Sahrawi people on their future. 

    The security council then rejected a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission for a year. France and the UK — the two other permanent Security Council members — along with eight non-permanent members, backed the US resolution. 

    The end of the UN mission is undeniably better for Morocco than the Polisario Front, the political wing of the Sahrawi independence movement.

      <title>Rural voters were feeling left behind before the midterms, poll shows</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy</link>
      <description><p>Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base</p><p>Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.</p><p>Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jul/07/cost-of-living-poll-groceries-gas">affordability crisis</a>, particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices. By October, 61% of voters <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/voters-economy-cost-of-living-prices-poll">believed</a> the country was experiencing a recession, even though technically it wasn’t.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears</link>
      <description><p>Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/04/midterm-elections-results-senate-house-michigan-maine-mississippi-latest-updates">US midterm elections – live updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/explainer-midterms-trump-us-global-economy-markets">After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?</a></p></li></ul><p>US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a>, lifted by hopes that <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.</p><p>The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&amp;P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/03/midterm-election-results-live-updates">won control</a> of the Senate and the House of Representatives.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires</link>
      <description><p>It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness</p><p>Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. Even some economists agree. The Nobel prize-winning economists Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton once <a href="https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1011492107">proposed that</a> rising income increased people’s emotional wellbeing only up to a ceiling of about $115,000 in today’s money.</p><p>They probably hadn’t met many billionaires. The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word. But they will try every trick in the book to hang on to their stash and woe betide the tax authority that tries to lay a finger on their treasure.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 05 Nov 2026 22:41:31 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[US stocks drop sharply as Democrats win raises fears about AI investment ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/us-stocks-drop-sharply-as-democrats-win-raises-fears-about-ai-investment/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/us-stocks-drop-sharply-as-democrats-win-raises-fears-about-ai-investment/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 22:16:45 +0000US stocks shed $3.2 trillion (€2.85 trillion) in a day of chaotic trading which saw the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 plunge 6.4 per cent after the Democrats’ sweeping midterm election victory upended Wall Street’s mammoth AI bet.

The market value drop on the broad S&P 1500 Composite index on Thursday was among the biggest wipeouts since the turn of the millennium as investors rushed out of shares linked to AI.

The rout came amid fears that Democrats’ stunning victory over Donald Trump’s Republicans in Tuesday’s midterms would prompt a slowdown in the AI spending boom that has driven Wall Street to record highs this year.

“[Investors] are throwing in the towel and indiscriminately liquidating,” said Adam Crisafulli, president of market research group Vital Knowledge.

Selling in the tech sector was brutal, with Nvidia, the chipmaker most closely associated with the AI surge, tumbling 9.3 per cent, pushing its market value down more than $400 billion. The benchmark S&P 500 lost 4.4 per cent, its worst session since April 2025 in a session marked by big swings. Its fall showed the selling spreading beyond AI stocks into the general market.

“With the blue wave, investors fear that peak [AI capital spending] is behind us,” said Charles-Henry Monchau, chief investment officer at Swiss private bank SYZ Group.

One hedge fund portfolio manager said the move appeared to be “de-grossing”, in which fast-money investors cut big positions.

“People are starting to get worried now, today the move was so swift,” said another hedge fund executive.

Investors fear that newly elected politicians who campaigned against data centres will hit the brakes on AI infrastructure development, upending Wall Street’s expectations for vast spending on chips, servers and facilities that have powered stocks to record highs this year.

“Guys who would normally be bargain hunting, excited by these low prices, they’re not jumping in ... everyone’s hiding out in cash,” said the chief executive of a New York brokerage.

Embattled Pete Hegseth may face impeachment next week

Vincent Mortier, the investment chief of Amundi, said the “honeymoon” gains for US stocks on the day after Democrats won control of Congress had been “very shortlived”.

He added that the tech repricing was “harsh and quick as the fundamental question marks resurface under the microscope of the new political US picture – data centres backlash, new regulation”.

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect from Michigan, has said there should be a “full-on pause” in frontier development, arguing that “you’re seeing the pace of technological development outpace the pace of safety”.

Incoming South Carolina senator Annie Andrews proposed a two-year ban on new data centre construction to stop communities “getting steamrollered” by “incredibly wealthy, powerful companies”.

Trump responds to US midterms defeat as Democrats win full control of the Texas House

Chipmakers were among Thursday’s biggest declines. Qualcomm dropped 9.5 per cent, Broadcom fell 10 per cent and Micron shed 17 per cent.

Elon Musk’s companies, which are both based in Texas, where Democrats won the race for governor and their first Senate seat for more than 30 years, had another bad day.

Tesla fell 10.8 per cent, adding to a 3.3 per cent drop on Wednesday, while SpaceX was down 9.1 per cent, on top of a 3.8 per cent drop the previous day. – The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Michael Nagle<![CDATA[Dublin liqueur distillery enters liquidation after failing to secure investment in restructuring]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/dublin-liqueur-distillery-enters-liquidation-after-failing-to-secure-investment-in-restructuring/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/dublin-liqueur-distillery-enters-liquidation-after-failing-to-secure-investment-in-restructuring/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 11:36:05 +0000Stillgarden Distillery, the Dublin 8-based independent producer of Italian amari liqueurs, has ceased trading and entered voluntary liquidation.

The company “has not succeeded” in a “lengthy search” conducted this year to raise new investment to sustain the business, it announced on Thursday morning. It had sought an experienced international managing director to lead the company, which sells its products in Ireland and Britain, to “the next stage of growth”.

“Despite months of work and conversations with a range of potential investors, no deal was secured, and the company could not afford to keep going on its own,” the distillery said in a statement announcing its closure.

Based on Tyrconnell Road in Inchicore, Dublin 8, Stillgarden Distillery was set up in February 2020 by husband and wife Pat O’Brien and Victoria Baird and their business partner Damien Heary.

It produced Irish amari, a herbal liqueur typically drunk as a digestif after dinner, as well as other similar products, and was sold in the UK through supplier Master of Malt.

Sales rose as the Covid-19 pandemic eased and reached close to €400,000 in 2023, according to the distillery. However, heightened production costs and a tightened market space forced the team to restructure in 2024, narrowing the range of products on offer just to break even.

Baird, the distillery’s managing director, said: “We have done everything we could to keep Stillgarden going.

“We made the business leaner, built a brand that people loved here and in the UK and put everything into finding the right investor to take it to the next level.

“What a small independent distillery needs is capital, and we simply could not keep funding it ourselves.”

Abridged financial accounts for the distillery’s parent company, Disruptive Spirits, from the 2024 financial year show the business owed substantial sums of money to its two directors.

The company made a €833,000 loss in income by the end of 2024, the accounts show, and received €60,000 in Government grants to support the business’ operations.

]]><![CDATA[Sony profits soar on the success of new Spider-Man movie]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/sony-profits-soar-on-the-success-of-new-spider-man-movie/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/sony-profits-soar-on-the-success-of-new-spider-man-movie/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 18:25:51 +0000Sony raised its annual profit forecast after reporting a 45 per cent increase in second-quarter operating profit, boosted by the success of the new Spider-Man movie.

The Japanese entertainment group reported operating profit of 622 billion yen (€3.6 billion) for the quarter and raised its full-year profit outlook by 9 per cent, beating analyst expectations, on the back of the performance of its movie and games segments.

Revenue at Sony’s film division rose 48 per cent year-on-year in the second quarter, “primarily due to the contribution of” Spider-Man: Brand New Day. The latest instalment in the long-running franchise has taken close to $2.5 billion worldwide, making it one of the biggest releases of all time.

Sony’s games division also posted a 9 per cent jump in revenues in the quarter, boosted by higher sales of games from Sony’s studios. Marvel’s Wolverine had sold 2.4 million copies as of the start of November, still far from breaking even but contributing to profits in the quarter, according to analysts.

The results come as Sony looks to convince investors of its strategic shift towards entertainment and the creation of original content.

The group is seeking to stitch together its gaming, anime, film and music businesses to build global franchises. Huge recent successes include The Last of Us, which was adapted from a PlayStation game into a popular HBO drama, and the animated film Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba.

Sony shares have risen more than a third from a low in June as investors have placed fresh bets on the strength of its entertainment businesses and the prospects for its gaming division.

The highly anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI this month is also propelling expectations since the PlayStation game is expected to capture a significant slice of sales.

“Spider-Man has been a massive hit and the market seriously underestimated just how well Sony’s movies business would perform. It’s a huge beat, with an upgrade to guidance to match,” said David Gibson, an analyst at MST Financial.

“Gaming was less exciting, but with Grand Theft Auto VI just two weeks away and pre-orders looking extremely strong, that could very well change quickly. The question is how much of that success is already priced into the shares,” he added.

Meanwhile, Japanese rival Nintendo disappointed analysts on Thursday, with operating profits declining 16 per cent in the second quarter as the new Switch 2 suffered from rising component costs and a lack of big new games.

Nintendo will hope that Thursday’s release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time – a remake of the smash-hit console game – will drive more sales heading into the crucial holiday period, say analysts.

Shares in Sony and Nintendo rose 7 and 6 per cent on Thursday, respectively, before the results were released. Investors are betting that more restrained investment in AI following the Democrats’ midterm wins in the US this week could ease pressure on memory chip prices and, in turn, lower production costs for their games consoles.

]]><![CDATA[Tech stocks plunge on AI regulation fears]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/tech-stocks-plunge-on-ai-regulation-fears/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/tech-stocks-plunge-on-ai-regulation-fears/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 18:34:25 +0000Poor results from microchip maker Qualcomm and fears that a Democrat majority US Congress could tighten artificial intelligence (AI) regulations sparked a fresh sell off in tech stocks on Thursday.

Technology-focused benchmarks tumbled. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index in the US had plunged 11 per cent by midafternoon Irish time.

Dublin

Greencoat Renewables added 0.87 per cent after reporting €11.9 million profit for the first half of the year.

London

The FTSE 100 gave back strong early gains on Thursday to close lower after the Bank of England increased interest rates and signalled that it could put up borrowing charges further.

Polar Capital Technology Trust fell 6.6 per cent to 543. Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust shed 4.8 per cent to 1,434. Allianz Technology Trust was down 7.1 per cent at 602.

Guinness parent Diageo toasted a 3.2 per cent rise to 1,871.5 after reporting stronger-than-expected quarterly results. A decline in sales in North America proved less than feared, allowing the company to reiterate forecasts for full-year profits.

The London-listed brewer and distiller, which also owns Smithwicks ale, Rockshore lager, and premium scotches, Lagavulin and Caol Ila, said net sales grew 1.2 per cent to $4.93 billion (€4.39 billion) in the three months ended September 30th from $4.88 billion during the same period in 2025.

Europe

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index closed 0.38 per cent lower at 654.87 points after a rally in the continent’s equities fizzled out once US markets opened.

The shift dragged the index back from close to an all-time high in earlier trading. Regional bourses were mixed, however, with French and ​Spanish benchmark indexes ending higher.

Technology stocks collectively fell 3.2 per cent to their lowest level in nearly two months, tracking losses on Wall Street where the tech-heavy Nasdaq was ⁠poised to confirm a correction by Thursday evening.

Computer chip-linked stocks were among the biggest decliners on the Stoxx 600. Soitec slumped ‌16.7 per cent, while ​Infineon fell 8.5 per cent and Aixtron declined 9.8 per cent. AI heavyweight ASML retreated 6.6 per cent and Siltronic slid 12.3 per cent.

Defence stocks fell 2.6 per cent, weighed down by a 16.1 per cent drop in Rheinmetall after the company cut its 2026 sales forecast for the second time in three months.

Air France-KLM gained 12 per cent after beating third-quarter earnings expectations, while renewable energy firm Orsted rose 3.5 per cent after its strong ‌results.

Aker BP fell 5.6 per cent after BP sold a stake in the Norwegian oil and gas company.

New York

The tech-heavy US Nasdaq share index was on track for its worst day in 18 months after slumping by up to 5 per cent on Thursday on signs that the AI industry faced tougher regulation following this week’s US midterms elections.
