Nvidia, the chipmaker at the heart of the AI boom, was the top faller on the index, down 6.7 per cent, followed by bank Goldman Sachs, which fell 5.7 per cent. – Additional reporting by Press Association and Reuters

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Pharma giant Abbott told to pay €25,000 after dismissing scientist with endometriosis]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/abbott-must-pay-25000-to-scientist-with-endometriosis-humiliated-by-dismissal/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/abbott-must-pay-25000-to-scientist-with-endometriosis-humiliated-by-dismissal/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 17:21:16 +0000A scientist who said she tried to push through “excruciating” endometriosis pain while driving up to four hours a day for work for pharma giant Abbott – only to be “humiliated” when she was dismissed during her probationary period – has won €25,000.

The worker, who has more than a decade of industry experience and advanced postgraduate qualifications, told the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) last year how she was given just 10 minutes to pick up her belongings and get off site after being told she failed her probation.

She said she was reduced to “crying all the way back” in a colleague’s arms during the drive home.

Now Abbott Ireland Ltd has been ordered to pay the worker €25,000 as compensation for discriminatory dismissal on disability grounds in breach of the Employment Equality Act 1998.

The worker, referred to as X, was hired by Abbott in 2024 and spent just short of six months working in an office at an Abbott siteanalysing test data, but was deemed to have failed her probation and was let go that autumn, the tribunal heard.

The company’s representative, Fiona Egan of the Irish Business and Employers’ Confederation, said X failed her probation for “conduct and performance” following a number of instances of lateness and uncertified absences from work.

It had “nothing to do with her condition”, she said.

Shaun Boylan, for X, said the firm’s policy of refusing to allow probationary employees to work from home was “implicitly discriminatory” against his client as it put accommodations for her disability “on hold for six months”.

X, who was afforded anonymity by the WRC at a hearing last year, said she had been diagnosed with stage-two endometriosis in 2022, a condition affecting the female reproductive organs.

She said it caused her “debilitating pain”, accompanied by “nausea, fainting and dizziness”, which was at its worst during the seven to eight days of her period and required prescription-only codeine and opiate painkillers to manage.

The daily drive from X’s home to the Abbott site was “coming up on a four-hour commute to work every day”, adjudication officer Brian Dolan remarked during the hearings on her case.

X said she thought at first she should “just endure” the commute. Her evidence was that she was “promised in the interview that it would be a hybrid role” and that she turned down roles elsewhere with a five-day-a-week on-site commitment because of that.

Six weeks after she started, a “sudden” department-wide meeting was called and a manager declared “there would be no more work from home possible” at the site, barring the “possibility” of one day a week, she said.

X said she was in “excruciating pain” that day and found the message “difficult to take”. She told the WRC she went straight to her team leader “in visible distress, with tears in my eyes” and proceeded to tell him she had endometriosis.

She said her team leader was “empathetic” and “supportive” at that stage and gave her an assurance that a “one week in, one week out” work from home arrangement would be possible, but only once her probation was finished.

Making it in for an on-site team meeting at 9.30am meant setting out from home at 6.30am or 6.45am, X said.

More than seven weeks before a probationary caution letter being issued in her final weeks on the job, X was late eight times and absent without a medical cert on three occasions, leading to an occupational health referral.

X said a senior manager told her at one stage that “the company cannot offer more than one day work from home past your probation” and urged her to find somewhere to live closer to the site.

An occupational health report, which went to her line manager two weeks before she lost her job, stated that the complainant had a chronic condition and urged a two-day-a-week remote work arrangement, the tribunal noted.

The probation review continued into the following month, ending when her team leader called her into a conference room and read out a letter stating that her employment was being terminated, she said.

The only reason stated was: “Your standard of performance has not met company expectations.”

“I asked why. [My team leader] said, ‘Everything is in the letter’,” X said.

After saying she could not continue with the meeting, a company human resources officer told her an outstanding pay matter could be handled by email and gave her “10 minutes to leave, to grab [my] stuff and leave the premises”.

“Everyone was crying in the car,” she said. “I hugged my colleague in the car, and kept crying all the way back to Dublin,” she said.

Questioned on why she had not disclosed her condition in a pre-employment questionnaire, X said she was “scared to be discriminated against” by having the job offer withdrawn.

She said she had disclosed her diagnosis to a company nurse at a separate assessment 10 days into her employment, but said expressly that she did not require accommodations to work in a lab.

In his decision, adjudicator Brian Dolan said Abbott did not discriminate against X by failing to accommodate her disability during her employment.

However, despite the occupational health report linking her absences to her health, the pharma firm dismissed her without “further consideration” of her disability or how to resolve the matter without terminating her employment.

“I find that the complainant’s dismissal constituted an act of discrimination on the grounds of disability,” he wrote.

He ordered Abbott to pay €25,000 in compensation to the woman.

]]>Christopher Dilts<![CDATA[Virgin Media TV remained in profit last year despite falling advertising revenues]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/virgin-media-tv-remained-in-profit-last-year-despite-falling-advertising-revenues/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/virgin-media-tv-remained-in-profit-last-year-despite-falling-advertising-revenues/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 13:40:20 +0000Virgin Media Television posted a second consecutive year of operating profit last year despite falling revenues stemming from a continuing decline in spot advertising.

New accounts for Virgin Media Television Ltd (VMTV), the company behind the Virgin Media One channel and the Virgin Media Player, revealed that operating profits at the company, which is owned by billionaire media mogul John Malone’s Liberty Global, dropped by more than 97 per cent to €544,000 last year.

]]>Alain Jocard<![CDATA[Europe is again eyeing Ireland’s corporate tax revenue]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/05/europe-is-again-eyeing-irelands-corporate-tax-revenue/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/05/europe-is-again-eyeing-irelands-corporate-tax-revenue/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:39:36 +0000The EU is struggling to put together a budget package for the next seven years. This has left European Council president António Costa casting around for new sources of funds that can shore up the budget sums by increasing the bag of tax resources over which the EU has direct control.

The risk for Ireland is that corporate taxes are again in the frame. And as the biggest EU recipient of multinational corporate taxes, the Government could befacing another diplomatic battle to protect Irish revenues.

Costa has been looking at options that would funnel some tax revenues away from countries where multinationals now pay their tax – including Ireland – into the central EU pot.

In focus, in particular, are the payments resulting from the recent OECD corporate tax reform plan, which has provided yet another boost to Irish coffers. It is part of an old story of Europe eyeing Irish corporate tax receipts, but the recent growth in revenues has left Ireland particularly exposed.

The picture is still a little muddy as Costa, who is charged with seeking a compromise on the budget, tries to put together a plan to satisfy demands from the “frugal” northern countries – led by Germany – who are seeking lower national contributions and a cut to the proposed size of the budget – and eastern and southern states fighting to protect the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and cohesion funding.

But the issue may be raised at next week’s informal summit of EU leaders in Dublin, in advance of what is meant to be a crunch summit in Brussels at the end of the month.

The backdrop – Costa’s coffers

EU member states are trying to agree a budget – or so-called multiannual financial framework – to cover the years from 2028 to 2034.

Ireland, as EU president, had put forward a proposal for an 8 per cent cut in the original €1.76 trillion proposal (in 2025 prices) by the European Commission. But this was criticised by all sides, leading Taoiseach Micheál Martin to observe it was an exercise in trying to “reconcile the irreconcilable”.

Ireland’s EU presidency proposes budget cut of €141bn for the bloc

The job of seeking compromise now passes to Costa, who has to try to bang heads together among EU leaders.

As part of this, he is looking for new sources of what are called “own resources”, which is funding that goes directly to Brussels rather than forming part of annual contributions from member states.

The proposal – target companies

To try to bridge the gap between the desire of the “frugal” countries to contribute less and the need for a bigger EU centralised budget, there has been a range of proposals to raise additional taxes that would go directly to Brussels, or divert existing taxes in their direction.

The European Parliament, for example, has proposed a range of measures, including a new gambling levy and a special tax on cryptocurrency.

And the idea of a levy on the revenues of companies with sales of more than €100 million has been circulating in the discussions, though it is strongly opposed by Germany.

To try to break the deadlock, there has been a series of reports – including in Politico and a number of special online tax services – that Costa’s team are looking at diverting some of the additional funding resulting from the OECD tax deal to the central EU budget.

Sources in Dublin confirm this has been floated, but say a firm proposal has not yet been made. But, with strong French support, it looks likely to emerge in discussions in the next few weeks on the new budget.

The exposure – Ireland’s extra revenue

Ireland has done remarkably well over the past decade as a result of two OECD corporate tax deals.

The initial 2015 agreement led companies to change their tax planning in a way where more funds fell to be taxed in Ireland. (This happened largely because many relocated intellectual property assets from offshore havens to Ireland).

The latest OECD deal – agreed in 2021 – had been expected to be a mixed bag for Ireland.

The State stood to lose from a part of the deal that would have moved some of the taxing rights on corporate profits away from countries such as Ireland – where they have corporate headquarters – to bigger European countries where digital multinationals did much of their business.

In the end,this part of the OECD deal has fallen through.

The second part of the OECD deal set a minimum rate of 15 per cent for tax on profits of big multinationals. Although this has only been partially implemented – the US has important exemptions – the 15 per cent rate was mandated as a minimum in the EU.

Ireland thus has a basic 12.5 per cent corporate profits tax and an additional 2.5 per cent charge on the biggest companies. It is this additional money that Costa appears most likely to have his eye on.

The mechanics – as yet uncertain

Various sources say Costa is testing the waters at EU capitals and so the shape of what he may propose is unclear.

However, he has clear French support for a move on corporate tax, and this will put Ireland firmly in the frame. The amount Ireland will collect as a result of the 2.5 per cent charge is significant – the Fiscal Council has said it could amount to some €5 billion, or about 13 per cent of total expected corporate tax revenues this year.

Former OECD tax head Pascal Saint-Amans told Politico the sense of the new plan was that multinational activity in Ireland was about managing their business in EU markets.

And so it could make sense to redistribute tax in this way – in effect, it would have a similar impact to the part of the 2021 OECD plan that has never gone ahead to redistribute some taxing rights away from countries such as Ireland.

The odds – still unclear

Ireland, along with other EU member states, has fought off several previous proposals to effectively pool elements of corporate tax revenues into a central EU budget.

Those with greyer hairs may recall the alphabet soup that was the proposal for the common corporate tax base (CCTB), which later evolved into the common consolidated corporate tax base (CCCTB). These circulated for more than a decade before being formally withdrawn in 2023.

Tax has primarily been a national competence in the EU – countries decide what to tax and by how much. And, ultimately, countries have a veto on tax issues, and the EU budget plan must be agreed by all 27 member states.

But a new focus on corporate tax would be uncomfortable for Ireland, forcing the Government to use up political capital resisting any plan and again underlining the extraordinary bounty flowing into the Irish exchequer.

Other EU countries argue that some of this is at their expense.

Donald Trump has argued likewise. And a newly energised US Congress may again start probing where and how big American companies pay their taxes.

Changes in the fortunes or plans of the big multinationals who pay tax here remain a big risk in the years ahead. But so do politics in the US and around Europe.

Ireland’s revenues are now so enormous that they are attracting way more international attention than the Government would like.

]]><![CDATA[Hybrid working isn’t the problem, it is how to manage it]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/05/the-pitfalls-of-hybrid-working-when-managers-are-left-on-their-own-to-deal-with-staff/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/05/the-pitfalls-of-hybrid-working-when-managers-are-left-on-their-own-to-deal-with-staff/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:49:00 +0000

Break-up songs like Prince’s Nothing Compares 2 U (a smash for Sinéad O’Connor), Dolly Parton’s I Will Always Love You (ditto Whitney Houston) and Miley Cyrus’s Flowers have long been popular culture staples. But who knew that breaking up with full-time office work would be so agonising for business culture – and especially for the line managers left to negotiate the wreckage?

Workplace tension continues between leaders who demand a return to the office and workers who want flexibility to help defray the cost of living, and to better cope with commuting times and care commitments.

The whole debate about whether or not hybrid, or remote, is actually workable, is the wrong question to ask, says Tatiana Andreeva, professor in organisational behaviour at Trinity Business School, who studies hybrid work and collaboration.

Instead, how can employers embrace hybrid in a way that creates sustainable value for the business, employees and society?

More than a third of the labour force now works either a hybrid arrangement or a fully remote one – accounting for an estimated 530,000 people – according to a forthcoming report from the National Economic and Social Council.

In 2026, about 35 per cent of the labour force worked from home either usually or sometimes, whereas before the Covid-19 pandemic, only about 14 per cent of employees worked from home to some extent.

Even though this is a relatively new way of working, those managing these arrangements may be largely left on their own – without training, support or even simple tips for communicating with hybrid workers.

New report on impact of hybrid working in Ireland to deliver its findings

The problem isn’t with remote work itself, but in how it’s managed, says Andreeva. “We can make it work if the people who are actually managing it on a daily basis – line managers – are better prepared. If we fix this group, the spillover effects for the organisation will be amazing.”

The resources already exist to make this possible too, she says. Grow Remote, for example, is a government-supported social enterprise that helps employers, managers and remote workers thrive through online training, resources and community connections.

New ways of working

In the past decade, line managers have taken on more HR responsibilities (onboarding, interviews, appraisals), but the power to manage hybrid work policies and team-oriented ways of working has been taken from them. Andreeva, Dr Jordi Trullen (ESADE Business School) and Jim Copeland (Maynooth University) interviewed 36 line managers across 32 organisations to understand their shifting responsibilities, their reaction to hybrid work policies and the obstacles they face.

Most of these qualitative in-depth interviews were with line managers working in US multinationals in Ireland. The study found that hybrid policies were mostly set centrally without consulting line managers, who then had to adapt them informally with little training or information on how to manage hybrid teams.

The interviews revealed some worrying trends. Line managers reported that their organisations gave them no say on remote policies, no insights into remote workers’ schedules, and no training or support on how to manage them. They’re flying blind while being expected to deliver the same or better levels of productivity.

Although line managers are expected to support or reinforce compliance, they were typically not given access to live or recent individual-level attendance data or monitoring tools. This limited their ability to intervene effectively or anticipate issues within the team.

Many managers also expressed concerns over the official reasons provided for returning to the office, as these were often not convincing. This, and getting little or no notice on policy-change announcements, limited managers’ ability to persuade their subordinates to follow the policy.

Managers identified persistent challenges with hybrid work co-ordination. Yet few received any structured training or support on how to manage these dynamics.

“The line managers feel that there’s an assumption in the organisation that if you were a manager during Covid that you know how to do it, and that is why training doesn’t come up,” says Andreeva.

Hybrid teams require complex co-ordination due to staggered schedules and individual exceptions. But, instead of reporting these difficulties to leadership, line managers operated from a place of fear, and often withheld details of these operational challenges to prevent a full return to working from the office for everyone.

Managing hybrid

Andreeva has been working on a book chapter with Prof N Sharon Hill of George Washington University School of Business to help address the information deficit in understanding hybrid work dynamics and best practices. Hill developed the CAARE framework (configuration, autonomy-alignment, relationships, equity) in 2023 and her work was published in MIT Sloan Management Review.

‘One of the managers in our study added 15 minutes with no work-related agenda to daily team meetups to allow the team to connect casually, compensating for lost in-person informal lunchtime chats’

Tatiana Andreeva, Trinity Business School

The CAARE framework helps organisations and managers think through and implement remote and hybrid ways of working with their team.

Configuration

Remote and hybrid teams have a different shape and rhythm compared to teams that work entirely from the office. Configuration is a strategic way to establish agreements on how members will work together.

What’s the real reason your boss wants you back in the office?

“Team agreements may, for example, specify core hours of availability, expected response times for communications, and procedures for providing updates on work status,” says Hill.

Atlassian and Dropbox designed tool kits for managers to help them co-develop these charters with their teams. Managers are encouraged to review these charters regularly with teams as employee preferences and situations may change.

Autonomy and alignment

To be effective, there needs to be a balance between individual autonomy and team alignment. Grow Remote found that some companies do this in a quick and clever way that works best for their team.

NearForm trained their managers to introduce asynchronous daily stand-ups. Each morning, team members answer four questions in Slack (How are you feeling? What have you done? What will you do today? Do you need help?). The manager scans responses for blockers instead of holding a daily call. The regularity of these check-ins ensures alignment, while also giving employees autonomy in where and when they work.

Relationships

“One of the managers in our study added 15 minutes with no work-related agenda to daily team meetups to allow the team to connect casually, compensating for lost in-person informal lunchtime chats; another added a five-minute fun fact slot in weekly meetings, inviting one of the team members to share something that you wouldn’t know about them,” Andreeva says.

In both cases, the manager’s aim was to provide space for informal connection and relationship-building.

]]><![CDATA[After the SuperValu cyberattack, might your smart fridge be the next target? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:41:50 +0000Do you feel differently about your smart fridge?

The high-tech home hub allows you to check what food you have in, suggest recipes, and manage the family calendar, should you be able to afford its not-insignificant price tag.

But this week’s cyberattack on Supervalu’s refrigeration systems might be forcing people to re-evaluate its position in their home.

Where could the next attack come from?

You might equally be eyeing your connected coffeemaker warily, worried about what it could be getting up to behind your back. You might consider unplugging the robot vacuum cleaner in case it goes rogue while you are out on the school run.

Jokes aside, the recent spate of attacks on seemingly harmless systems should give us pause for thought. The problem with many of these connected devices is that as soon as you hook anything up to the internet, it opens up a chink in your armour , no matter how hard we try to lock it down.

It is a trade-off that we might not be aware we are making at the time – but it is a common thread in the modern world. For the sake of convenience, we give up a little security. Even with the most diligent company in charge of maintaining the security of the appliances, there is always a risk that something will go wrong. And with the growth in artificial intelligence (AI), the chance of a previously undetected vulnerability rearing its head has suddenly been magnified.

You might wonder why hackers would want to attack a smart home device in the suburbs of Dublin. While we may not have thousands of euro of stock to destroy, or disposable income to pay out ransoms, we do have something that is valuable: our data. And that, as we know, is worth a lot of money in the right – or wrong – hands.

There is also the chance that our smart home devices, unpatched and open to exploitation, may be used as part of an attack on a high-value target.

Stop the bots: Six key steps to securing your smart home

In recent days, a joint operation between public and private partners in the tech industry took down a global botnet that had been hidden in set-top boxes across 200 countries. The botnet, which was placed on the devices before they were sold, surreptitiously used the set-top boxes and internet connections of those unlucky enough to have installed them in their homes.

This is not a new threat. Botnets have been carrying out large-scale attacks for years. One example: in 2016, the Mirai botnet took over up to 560,000 unsecured or weak cameras, printers, and DVR players and knocked out Twitter, Reddit, and Netflix, among others.

So what can we do to protect ourselves? Besides cutting off the connection, that is, although you could argue there is no compelling need to have an oven or coffee maker with an internet connection.

There is some help on the way from the bureaucrats, with various rules regarding security being implemented at an EU level, forcing manufacturers to adopt a secure-by-design approach. But we can’t rely on them to fully shield us from all the risks.

There are ways to protect ourselves: keeping up to date with software releases to patch up any security holes is a given;buying reputable brands rather than settling for cheap, unbranded technology from online marketplaces is another. Changing the default passwords on devices is another tip from security experts.

But we need to be aware of what could be coming down the line.

Anthropic recently warned of another threat: that AI models are becoming so smart and small in terms of storage requirements that they could copy themselves into places you might not suspect – such as your smart fridge.

That could create an army of smart botnets that could, in theory, be commanded to launch attacks without needing a data centre to run from. And, the experts argue, that would be one that is very difficult to battle, because there is no centralised point from where the attack has been launched.

Of course it is never as simple as it looks. The scenario proposed by Anthropic was a test rather than a real-world incident, and the end result – a model that replicates itself – is more of a ‘could’ than a ‘did’. The model didn’t have to break in as such, although we are often so lax about security on these connected devices that it wouldn’t have presented a huge barrier if that had been the case.

There are a few lessons to learn here.

Take the claims of AI companies about the power and potential of their technology with a grain of salt, for both good and bad.

But perhaps, to be safe, you might also consider limiting smart technology to the essentials. Sometimes the trade-off just isn’t worth it.

Caulfield, who did not name individual businesses, indicated that most unlicensed players halted operations after receiving initial cease and desist warnings.

“We have not been to the High Court,” she said.

Many black market operators ignore the legal safeguards applied to licensed businesses, including a ban on the use of credit cards and age checks, Caulfied pointed out.

Almost four in 10 people who open online accounts initially to bet on horse racing or sport go on to other forms of gambling, including casino games, slot machines and lotteries, the research shows.

Online betting companies cross-sell casino and slot machine games to these customers. Lunn argued that this drew them to forms of gambling where customers had a higher risk of developing problems.

One quarter were trying to reduce their gambling or wanted to do so, but one third of that group were betting the same amounts or more than a year previously.

The Irish Bookmakers Association welcomed the report, saying it had always insisted that regulation should be based on evidence.

The ESRI published Patterns of Online and In-person Gambling in Ireland by Deirdre Robertson, Diarmaid Ó Ceallaigh, Shane Timmons and Pete Lunn, on Wednesday.

“Curtailment will increase markedly when offshore wind comes online. Hydrogen, which can be produced from this otherwise wasted electricity and stored, has the potential to provide backup power for large energy users in peak times.”

He explained that hydrogen fuel cells produce electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen atoms. The hydrogen reacts with oxygen across an electrochemical cell, similar to a battery, to produce electricity, water and small amounts of heat.

“In addition to being utilised in the European energy transition, hydrogen needs to continue to develop a mutually beneficial and circular relationship with large energy users such as data centres, aviation and their respective supply chains.

“As Ireland delivers its EU presidency and partnering with the Clean Hydrogen Partnership, H2 Summit 2026 in Cork will focus on turning ambition into co-ordinated action on demand creation, system security and EU‑aligned deployment.”

Valérie Bouillon-Delporte, executive director of the European Commission’s Clean Hydrogen Partnership, said the summit comes at a timely moment for Europe and Ireland as it will showcase some of Ireland’s leading operational projects and pathways to future deployment.

“Convened during Ireland’s EU Council presidency, the summit sends a strong signal that clean hydrogen remains part of the conversation on energy security, industrial competitiveness and resilient infrastructure,” said Bouillon-Delporte.

7-9: Since 1862, O’Connell’s pub has traded from Eyre Square. It remained in the O’Connell family until 2006, when Maureen O’Connell nominated St Vincent de Paul as the main beneficiary in her will. Global benchmark Brent has surged more than 70 per cent this year as the nine-month war disrupted flows from the Gulf and upended energy markets. Diesel and gasoline prices have also rallied, including in the US, potentially influencing the outcome of the midterms. - Bloomberg

The Irish Army obviously needs vehicles but seems to have shaped its future role around turning itself into a conventional armoured brigade that can – don’t say it too loudly – fight alongside other European armies in the sort of battle groups that have been potentially rendered obsolete by the conflict in Ukraine.

The other task that is envisioned for the Army once it’s tooled up is deployment overseas on UN missions. There has not been a UN deployment authorised since 2011, and the mandate for Unifil – Ireland’s most significant deployment in Lebanon – is not being renewed when it runs out at the end of the year.

Not accepting the regrettable but real decline in the global role of the UN is also tantamount to fighting the last war.

The real elephant in the room is where are we going to find the soldiers to fight in these new tanks. The Defence Forces simply does not provide an attractive career for many. That might change. Driving tanks and going overseas are the sort of things that professional soldiers like doing.

Dangers on a train: Russia’s improved drones pose new threat to Ukrainian rail users

But the question that nobody seems to want to ask, however, is whether reshaping the Defence Forces around new armoured vehicles is really the most effective and economical way to defend our land and sea borders now that drones and missiles dominate the battlefield.

Paradoxically, the neglect of the Defence Forces over the years presents Ireland with a unique opportunity to skip a generation of military technology and create a force able to fulfil this goal at a cost that is realistic. And one that could attract the best and brightest engineering and technological talent.

‘Whatever Trump and Putin agree, we’ll fight the invaders’: Inside the dugouts powering Ukraine’s drone war

Our complete lack of a domestic arms industry means that, unlike our larger European partners, we are not trapped by history. Big countries end up locked into feeding their arms manufacturers in what former US president and D-Day commander Dwight Eisenhower dubbed the military-industrial complex.

This includes the French and hence their enthusiasm for selling us tanks. The cost will be enormous. As well as the upfront price, put at about €1 billion, we will be tied into a long-tailed maintenance contract with the French suppliers, which could bring the costs to many multiples of this.

Belgium bought 442 similar vehicles for €1.6 billion, but the lifetime cost is put at €14 billion, or €3.6 million per vehicle. It’s a lot of money for something that could be knocked out by a drone costing a couple of hundred euro.

The potential for marine drones to help police the 880,000sq km of seabed under Ireland’s jurisdiction, including vital submarine cables, is equally obvious for a Naval Service that faces real difficulties crewing its ships.

What adds to the paradox is that we already have a nascent drone industry, but seem determined to stamp it out. Manna Aero, the best-known Irish drone-maker, has abandoned attempts to set up a drone-based delivery service here, citing the lack of a national drone strategy. This was after it was refused planning permission by Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council for a drone delivery hub.

The main issue was concern over the intrusive nature of drones, which will remain a significant issue for drone deliveries in urban areas. Not so much on battlefields.

Manna is a relatively small player, but its technological abilities are well regarded. It is not in the military drone space and has expressed no interest in the area publicly. To date, it has raised something north of €100 million. But as the Ukraine war has shown, the technology is fundamentally dual-use. Manna shows what can be achieved.

The question as to whether Ireland’s security would be better served by investing €14 billion into making our own air and sea drones is one well worth asking before signing a cheque for new tanks.

]]><![CDATA[Memo to AI: Remember when secretaries were seen as the biggest threat to jobs?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/memo-to-ai-lessons-from-the-rise-and-fall-of-secretarial-skills/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/memo-to-ai-lessons-from-the-rise-and-fall-of-secretarial-skills/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 05:34:00 +0000At a congress of shorthand writers held in Cincinnati almost 150 years ago, a stenographer called Helen T Pierson took to the stage to rebut male clerks’ growing protests that an influx of women threatened their job security. She took issue, in particular, with the misogynistic argument that women were undercutting men’s salaries because they were willing to work for less pay.

“The injustice of underpaying [women] is so gross and so palpable that it seems an impossibility that such a wrong should continue to exist,” Pierson told the mainly male audience. “It is hard and unfair in the extreme that a woman should be underpaid simply because she is a woman, and is not only unfair, but is calculated to do much harm.”

As with software and AI today, the mass adoption of shorthand and typing changed work habits and roles. But not all workers benefited. As new technology sweeps away the last vestiges of these older office productivity tools, what can we learn about how they were applied and misapplied?

First, try not to be too optimistic.

By the 1880s, supercharged by the rapid spread of office work, the typewriter and shorthand – the 2,000-year-old technique of using written symbols to speed the recording and transcription of speech – had combined to create new job opportunities for many women.

Before office work expanded in the US and Europe, social norms confined most of them to traditional “female roles” such as teaching or domestic service. But shorthand and especially typing were marketed as particularly suited to the female mentality and physique. By 1900, three-quarters of shorthand typists in the US were women – hence the distress of male clerks. Their protests were in vain. By 1930, 95 per cent of the US profession were women.

Yet shorthand and typing were a double-edged sword. Given a chance to enter the workforce, some women thrived. For instance, many British suffragists and suffragettes were expert typists who used their office skills as levers of emancipation, for instance, to prepare, print and distribute leaflets.

Secretarial skills also helped the first women stockbrokers, journalists and publishers break into their professions. Others enjoyed secretarial work simply for the flexibility and cash it provided to develop other career paths.

But many shorthand typists were consigned to life under a very low glass ceiling, far removed from the rosy imaginings of the late 19th century’s women pioneers. The determination and sacrifices required to progress in full-time paid work were sometimes too great.

The second lesson is that the intervention of aggressive consultants, selling technology on grounds of efficiency, is often bad for the people at the sharp end of that implementation.

By the 1910s, “scientific managers”, inspired by consultant Frederick Winslow Taylor’s mechanistic push to make manufacturing more efficient, were putting speedometers on typewriters to assess productivity. One Taylor disciple, William Henry Leffingwell, author of 1917’s Scientific Office Management, obsessed over the best way secretaries should arrange a desk (“keeping stationery in desk drawers is [a] source of waste motion”), how long it should take to insert a sheet of paper in a typewriter (three one-hundredths of a minute), and whether it paid to take paper clips off correspondence before filing (it depends: it takes 10 minutes to remove one pound of clips, he calculated).

Leffingwell was naturally a big advocate of the typing pool, which grouped shorthand typists together rather than relying on “small groups of uncontrolled stenographers throughout the office who work only part of their time on letters and part on miscellaneous clerical tasks and, as is often the case, sit in absolute idleness at other times”.

Historian Lucienne Boyce, who worked as a temporary secretary in the 1970s, says: “The whole image of the typing pool was of a factory, and the women became instruments ... just as you keep workers down in a factory, by giving them a tiny bit of job to do.” Boyce later became a careers adviser and saw how rarely men were directed down the secretarial path.

This was a world where “bosses, almost always male, literally dictate to female clericals”, as academic Catherine Rankovic has put it. As the century progressed, the combination of complete control, a rigid focus on efficiency, and lower status sucked from the office what little autonomy and joy women had hoped they might achieve there. It created what sociologist Margery Davies called a “secretarial proletariat”.

Obstacles that stood in the way of these women included formal or informal marriage bars, inadequate or non-existent maternity leave or childcare options, and looming disparities between the pay and promotion opportunities offered to women, not to mention casual sexism and outright sexual harassment.

A third lesson is that the same forces that lead to the birth of one technology can also hasten its demise at the hands of the next wave of development. The earlier technology’s users are often the unwitting victims. The Dictaphone, the electric typewriter, the computer and the internet finally put paid to the typing pool and consigned shorthand dictation to the shredder of secretarial skills.

With the advent of the desktop personal computer, the typewriter became a “keyboard” and the association of typing with women’s work broke down. Executives started to realise the quickest route from the idea in their heads to the memo or letter was through their own fingertips. “Now computers have come along, and ‘typing’ is ‘keyboarding’. Suddenly, voila! Men can type,” Gloria Steinem, the feminist activist, said in a 2007 commencement address at her alma mater Smith College. “Gives you faith in men’s ability to change, doesn’t it?”

So the dream that many women nursed in the late 19th century – that innovations such as shorthand and typing would provide a route into the workplace and a launch platform for promotion – was, for many, a hollow one. Only in the 2020s did women managers start to outnumber secretaries in the list of most common roles for women in the US.

But there is a fourth, and more upbeat, lesson from the rise and fall of the secretarial proletariat. New technologies can create opportunities for a smaller number of workers to cultivate skills that enable them to shape better jobs for themselves.

Secretaries have morphed into high-value personal and executive assistants, for instance, increasingly sought after for their command of the newest office tools.

Rebecca Siciliano, managing director of agency Tiger Recruitment, says a lot of her clients “want someone [who] is AI and tech savvy”.

These assistants must provide the expert human touch needed to juggle diaries packed with virtual and in-person meetings, and to represent their boss inside and outside the business. They need to know when to delegate to bots the more mundane tasks of taking minutes or updating spreadsheets. The best command salaries of £85,000 annually, according to Siciliano. Some may rise to become chiefs of staff and operations managers.

Much has changed since Pierson made the case for women in the workplace. The manual typewriter is long gone in most offices. The smartphone and AI are eradicating the last remnants of need for written shorthand. The subject property comprises a four-storey over-basement midterrace Georgian office building extending to a net internal area of 310sq m (3,336sq ft). The building retains a number of its original period features, including its decorative coving and cornicing, sash windows, fireplaces and timber flooring.

Number 72 comes for sale fully let to law firm Michael Boylan Litigation on a new, 10-year, full repairing and insuring lease commencing in July 2026 at a passing rent of €120,000 a year. The lease has a tenant break option in July 2031 and incorporates consumer price index linked rent reviews.

Located between St Stephen’s Green and Ballsbridge, on one of the city centre’s most sought-after streets, the property is well connected by public transport. The street itself is served directly by several Dublin Bus routes while the Luas green line stops at Charlemont, St Stephen’s Green and Harcourt are all situated within a short walk of the property.

The immediate area is home to a number of big employers including LinkedIn, EY, Arthur Cox, AerCap and Addleshaw Goddard.

Jake Brodeur, who is handling the sale on behalf of Colliers, says: “72 Lower Leeson Street offers excellent opportunity to acquire a fully let Georgian office investment in a prime Dublin 2 location. The combination of a strong city centre address, attractive period accommodation and secure income profile should see significant interest from both private investors and high-net-worth individuals.”

Chinese fast fashion platform Shein has announced a €500 million (2.2 billion zloty) investment to expand its logistics centre in Poland, a move it says will create around 2,000 new jobs by the end of this year.

The announcement comes amid growing controversy over the impact of Chinese e-commerce platforms on European businesses and follows a recent decision by the European Union to introduce a special fee on low-value parcels sent from outside the EU and European Free Trade Area.

SHEIN investește 500 mil. euro în Polonia. Extinde hub-ul logistic europeanhttps://t.co/WNbib4dFta pic.twitter.com/KiI1AB4wFM

— Cristi Dorombach (@piticu21) November 4, 2026

The investment will expand Shein’s existing logistics facility in Magnice, near the city of Wrocław in southwestern Poland, which has been operating since 2022.

The expansion will bring total employment at the site to around 10,000 by creating 2,000 jobs in logistics, supply chain management, technology and warehouse operations, according to local news service Wroclaw.pl. The facility will also host 6,500 autonomous robots for sorting items.

Shein says that the move will help it cut delivery times in Europe, allowing some orders to arrive within 48 hours.

“This investment in Poland clearly demonstrates our commitment and belief in the potential of the European market,” said Leonard Lin, the firm’s global head of public affairs.

“Poland has become one of the pillars of our operations in Europe,” he added. “This latest investment is a testament to our confidence in the country’s potential, the competencies of its workforce, and its business environment.”

 

The expansion comes as Shein faces a tougher trading environment in Europe. Its sales in the region fell by 13.9% year-on-year to $3.77 billion in the second quarter, while net profit dropped by 67%.

The decline comes as the EU steps up efforts to curb the influx of low-cost imports from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which European retailers say pose unfair competition.

In July, the bloc introduced a €3 fee on parcels worth less than €150. From 1 November, a further €2 handling fee was added to all imported parcels, regardless of their value, to cover customs processing costs.

China overtook Germany to become Poland’s biggest source of imports for the first time in July, ending a period of around 35 years in which Germany had consistently held top spot https://t.co/U6rQwfEJ7I

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2026

Shein has also faced accusations of labour-law violations at its facilities in China, including concerns that it may use cotton produced through forced labour.

The company disputes many of the allegations, saying that it prohibits forced and child labour and regularly inspects working conditions at its suppliers.

China is an increasingly important trading partner in Poland. In July, it overtook Germany to become Poland’s largest source of imports for the first time, driven by rising purchases of cars, computer hardware and consumer goods.

]]> Six detained in Poland on suspicion of exporting military components to Russia https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/05/six-detained-in-poland-on-suspicion-of-exporting-military-components-to-russia/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 11:36:51 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106418

Poland has detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components. Investigators say that over 2 million zloty (€450,000) worth of equipment was smuggled into the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

The arrests, which took place on 21 October and 2 November, were announced on Thursday morning by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) and National Prosecutor’s Office.

🚨 ROSYJSKI WYWIAD. PRZEMYT CZĘŚCI DO PRODUKCJI UZBROJENIA. 6 ZATRZYMANYCH.@ABW_GOV_PL rozbiła grupę podejrzaną o działalność na rzecz rosyjskich służb specjalnych.

🔴6⃣ osób zatrzymanych,
🔴2⃣1⃣przeszukanych lokalizacji,
🔴 4⃣osoby z zarzutami szpiegostwa – wszystkie trafiły… pic.twitter.com/L90n3rf5rY

— ABW (@ABW_GOV_PL) November 5, 2026

Prosecutors report that all six suspects have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group that sought to export weapon components from Poland to Russia in violation of a ban on such trade.

Four of the suspects have also been charged under Poland’s espionage law, accused of acting on behalf of Russian intelligence in return for financial benefits. Those four individuals have been placed in pretrial detention. The other two were released with preventative measures put in place.

The ABW says that the criminal group “illegally supplied Russia with significant quantities of military components, including those used in the production of ammunition and weapons systems”.

“This type of activity may lead to the strengthening of the Russian arms industry and the military capabilities of the Russian Federation, and thus pose a serious threat to Poland’s security and interests,” wrote the agency.

 

Prosecutors say that the group operated at least between June 2023 and December 2025 in Poland, Lithuania and Russia. Members were responsible for procuring goods and transporting them to Kaliningrad, which borders Poland and Lithuania.

“Vehicles equipped with hidden compartments were used to transport the goods,” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The suspects repeatedly crossed the Polish-Russian border, and some of the transports were intercepted by Polish border guards.”

Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, revealed that the six suspects include five Polish citizens, aged 25 to 52, and one Russian woman, aged 37.

Onet, a leading news website, reports, based on unnamed sources, that the Russian citizen acted as a liaison between the group and the foreign intelligence agency behind the operation.

Funkcjonariusze @ABW_GOV_PL zatrzymali 6 osób podejrzanych o udział w zorganizowanej grupie przestępczej działającej przeciwko Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej. Wśród zatrzymanych jest pięciu Polaków w wieku od 25 do 52 lat i 37-letnia Rosjanka.
🛑 Sąd – pod zarzutem szpiegostwa -…

— Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 5, 2026

Poland has seen a huge rise in espionage cases in recent years. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined.

Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.

In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage.

]]> Polish far-right leader Braun to face second trial https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/05/polish-far-right-leader-braun-to-face-second-trial/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 09:45:21 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106399

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun will again stand trial, after prosecutors filed an indictment against him for a series of anti-Ukrainian, anti-Jewish, anti-LGBT and anti-EU acts committed during his presidential election campaign last year.

Braun is already separately on trial for a number of other alleged crimes, including an attack on a Jewish religious ceremony in parliament. He is also facing further charges for a range of other alleged offences.

Grzegorz Braun stanie przed sądem. Prokuratura Okręgowa w Warszawie skierowała dziś akt oskarżenia za zuchwałą kradzież flag Ukrainy w Białej Podlaskiej i Unii Europejskiej w Katowicach, zniszczenie wystawy LGBT w Sejmie oraz zniesławienie organizatorów akcji Żonkile i Muzeum…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 4, 2026

On Wednesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw announced that it had indicted Braun for four alleged crimes. It was able to do so after the European Parliament, where Braun sits as an MEP, stripped him of immunity earlier this year.

One of the charges, for criminal defamation, stems from Braun’s claim, during a televised presidential debate in April last year, that the yellow paper daffodils distributed each year in Warsaw to mark the anniversary of the 1943 Jewish Ghetto Uprising against German Nazi rule are “symbols of shame”.

Prosecutors say that Braun’s words were “extremely xenophobic, manipulative and aggressive”, and that they defamed the organisers of the daffodil campaign, in particular the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews in Warsaw.

During the same debate, Braun also warned about the “Judaisation” of Poland, saying that “Jews have far too much say in Polish affairs”. That prompted protests by some of his opponents, one of whom filed a notification to prosecutors.

 

Two other charges relate to thefts of flags. In one incident, Braun and his supporters removed a Ukrainian flag hanging outside city hall in the town of Biała Podlaska during a campaign event. In another, he removed a European Union flag from the industry ministry in the city of Katowice and set it on fire.

Braun regularly rails against what he calls the “Ukrainisation” of Poland, warning of the supposed dangers of having so many Ukrainian refugees and migrants in the country. He is also a vocal critic of the EU. On those and other issues, Braun’s rhetoric often echoes Russian propaganda.

The final charge, of destruction of property, relates to an incident in June 2025, when Braun vandalised an exhibition about the LGBT+ community in the Polish parliament. He regularly condemns what he calls the “perversions” of LGBT+ people, and has called for homosexuality to be criminalised.

The European Parliament has again stripped Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face charges of denying Nazi crimes.

The decision marks the sixth time it has lifted Braun’s immunity, and the second time for charges of Holocaust denial https://t.co/O9FN1YbchE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2026

The charges Braun faces carry prison sentences of up to five years in the case of destruction of property, and up to one year in the case of criminal defamation and theft.

Additionally, the deputy leader of Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, Roman Fritz, was indicted for assisting in the theft of the EU flag, while four other men (who have not waived their right to anonymity under Polish law) were indicted for their alleged roles in stealing both the EU and Ukrainian flags.

All four incidents for which Braun has been indicted took place when he was campaigning for the May 2025 presidential elections, in which he finished a surprise fourth, with 6.3% of the vote.

Since then, KKP has continued to perform strongly in polls, with its support currently standing at around 9%. If it obtained that kind of result at next year’s parliamentary elections, it would be likely to play a major role in deciding what kind of government could be formed.

Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now.

How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Much of Braun’s political brand has been built around provocative statements and actions. The politician is already on trial for his attack on a Jewish Hanukkah ceremony taking place in parliament, at which he put out the candles with a fire extinguisher.

In their statement on Wednesday, the Warsaw prosecutor’s office noted that the latest hearings in that trial had been cancelled after Braun presented a medical certificate justifying his absence.

However, the prosecutors pointed out that, last Friday, the day that the hearings had been due to begin, Braun attended a protest by opposition supporters outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw, which that evening had been taken over by government-backed judges.

Braun was pictured “jostling with police riot police, addressing the crowd and giving interviews”, showing “no signs of health problems that would prevent him from attending the hearing”, wrote the prosecutors. They have therefore asked the court to investigate the doctor who issued the medical certificate.

Polish political leaders have reacted to the results of Tuesday’s US midterm elections, in which the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans.

The outcome was welcomed by Poland’s ruling coalition, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk declaring that “democracy won”. The response was more muted from the right-wing opposition and the office of conservative President Karol Nawrocki, who is a Trump ally.

🚨 🇺🇸 Tusk gives Trump some great advice. But will the US president listen?

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk urged the US president to seek compromises after the Republicans' defeat and not to rely on vetoes as his main way of governing.

Trump had earlier threatened to become… pic.twitter.com/s3E6G5zIQT

— NEXTA (@nexta_tv) November 4, 2026

Tusk addressed the election results on Wednesday afternoon local time at a press conference alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš. “Today, democracy won in America,” said a smiling Tusk. “I love democracy; it is a beautiful thing.”

“As President Donald Trump himself said just after the election, the Democrats did a good job, and I really could not agree more with him this time,” added Tusk. “I hope that the result will stabilise the situation also in our region.”

Although the United States remains Poland’s most important security partner, Tusk’s government – a broad, pro-EU coalition that ranges from left to centre right – has at times had uneasy relations with the Trump administration.

It has been critical of Trump’s conciliatory approach towards Russia, his often tough stance on Ukraine, as well as his pursuit of US control over Greenland.

Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc.

Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU.

In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32.

Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41).

However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh.

Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47).

Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc.

 

One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU.

Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).

These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%.

“In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data.

Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27.

However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal.

He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction.

According to Wiech, the high tax burden also reflects the costs of transforming Poland’s energy sector while continuing to support coal-fired power stations and the state budget.

He says Poland needs “on the one hand, to fund the accelerated but delayed transformation and modernisation of the electricity sector; on the other hand, to maintain the fleet of coal-fired power stations; and thirdly, to contribute to the state budget”, which is struggling with persistently high deficits.

Wiech expects, however, that politicians will come under pressure to reduce electricity bills ahead of next year’s parliamentary election. However, there have also been regular tensions between the two countries, in particular over their difficult shared histories. This year has seen the two sides clash over the unresolved issue of large-scale massacres during World War Two.

Poland’s ambassador to the United Nations, Krzysztof Szczerski, has resigned, becoming the third Polish ambassador to do so since a government-backed move by a group of judges to take control of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw.

All three of the departing ambassadors were previously aides or advisers to former President Andrzej Duda, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. They have criticised the attempt to oust the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed to the court under PiS.

Following the resignations of Poland’s Ambassadors to China and Romania, Prof. Krzysztof Szczerski, Poland’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has also submitted his resignation.

All three are senior state officials and experienced diplomats who have served at the…

On Monday afternoon, foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór announced that Szczerski had “submitted a request to shorten his diplomatic mission at the UN”, where he has served as ambassador since 2021.

Szczerski’s resignation followed those of Jakub Kumoch, Poland’s ambassador to China, and Paweł Soloch, the Polish envoy to Romania, who quit their posts on Friday and Saturday, respectively.

While Szczerski has not yet commented on the reasons for his departure, Kumoch and Soloch made clear that their decisions were motivated by Friday’s move to suspend Święczkowski from the TK.

Soloch wrote that the “attempt to unlawfully take over the Constitutional Tribunal” left him with “no possibility of continuing to serve as ambassador”. Kumoch said his decision was a “matter of conscience”, as “there are certain things I cannot explain abroad without losing face, and I have no intention of speaking ill of Poland”.

Szczerski previously served as a member of the European Parliament for PIS. In 2015, he joined the chancellery of PiS-aligned President Duda, later becoming the head of his cabinet and then head of his International Policy Bureau.

Kumoch was a member of Duda’s National Development Council, an advisory body to the president, before serving as ambassador to Switzerland, Turkey, and then China. Soloch was the head of Duda’s National Security Bureau from 2015 to 2022.

On Monday, after Szczerski’s resignation, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski suggested that the three ambassadors had quit at the urging of the current president, Karol Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS.

Sikorski sardonically suggested that, in contrast to Polish ambassadors who quit in 1981 over the imposition of martial law despite “risking vengeance from the communist regime”, the newly resigned trio “will surely be handsomely rewarded for their heroic deeds”.

 

The developments are part of a much broader fallout from the crisis around the TK, which began on Friday evening when large numbers of riot police appeared outside the court.

It soon transpired that a group of eight judges appointed by parliament to the TK this year – but five of whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in – had entered the court and declared that Święczkowski had been suspended from his position for failing to fulfil his duties.

Święczkowski, who before becoming a TK judge previously served as a member of the former PiS government, declared their actions unlawful and an attempted “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the six other justices appointed when PiS was in government.

The developments have created an unprecedented situation at the TK. However, the court has been in crisis since 2015, when Duda and the then-PiS government – which came to power that year – unlawfully rejected three judges appointed by the former parliament and replaced them with three of their own.

The current government, a broad coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, does not recognise the TK due to those illegitimate judges and has ignored its rulings since replacing PiS in power in December 2023.

This year, Tusk’s coalition began appointing judges to fill vacancies on the court. It has condemned Nawrocki and Święczkowski for refusing to accept those judges, saying that their actions are unlawful.

Given those circumstances, Tusk and his government have argued that tough action is necessary to restore the legitimacy of the TK. On Saturday evening, Tusk gave an address to the nation declaring that there can be “no compromise” over the rule of law.

However, a number of legal experts – including many who were highly critical of PiS’s policies towards the TK and other courts – have expressed doubts over the manner in which Korwin-Piotrowska and her colleagues have sought to take control of the tribunal.

While the eight judges appointed by the ruling coalition this year are all expected to attend, those appointed under the PiS government appear likely not to.

RMF reports, based on unnamed sources, that Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW) and agencies from unnamed allied countries last week issued a warning that sabotage activities could take place on the Polish-Russian border, potentially including border violations by armed groups.

 

In a separate statement, the national police headquarters told RMF that the ongoing operation is “directly related to the situation taking place in our country today, that is, acts of sabotage…and the actions of eastern services”.

That was a reference to the activities of Russia and its ally Belarus, which have in recent years carried out a series of acts of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” against Poland and other countries in the region.

Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year.

Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries.

The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology.

The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males.

The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added.

“I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.”

Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas.

 

With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps.

The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees.

“Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.”

The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers.

Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022

The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out.

The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites.

President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis.

However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters.

pic.twitter.com/Gk4bPH1pJU

— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 31, 2026

On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw.

At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors.

The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her.

pic.twitter.com/sni7uvIVke

— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 30, 2026

Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”.

Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”.

Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”.

⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94

— Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) October 31, 2026

The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy.

That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate.

As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench.

 

That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court.

However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek.

Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal.

Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence.

At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker.

The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon.

Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners.

Szymon Hołownia, the founder of the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), confirmed on Saturday morning that his group would attend the talks. He also urged Tusk to sit down at the table with Nawrocki.

Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”.

On Saturday afternoon, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and a deputy prime minister, also revealed that he would personally attend the consultations with Nawrocki.

Tusk’s only comment so far has been a social media post saying that restoring the rule of law “requires decisive action”. His justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, announced on Friday evening that he was seeking to have Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution lifted.

On Saturday, speaking to broadcaster TVN, Żurek expressed support for the actions taken by Korwin-Piotrowska. He called Nawrocki’s behaviour at the TK “shameful” and said he “hoped prosecutors will take action, because it is unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way”.

Meanwhile, Tusk’s other main coalition partner, The Left (Lewica), announced on Saturday afternoon that it would not attend the talks with Nawrocki.

“One cannot accept an invitation from someone who is himself responsible for the current situation regarding the Constitutional Tribunal,” wrote Anna-Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus. “The TK is in the hands of independent judges. Politicians should not tell them what to do.”

New files relating to Lord Peter Mandelson’s appointment as US ambassador are expected to be published by Christmas, City AM can reveal.

The senior civil servant Cat Little has written to MPs, saying the Metropolitan Police has allowed the government to publish new files which were previously held back by the Metropolitan Police pending an ongoing investigation into Mandelson.

Little said the Met had previously asked the government not to publish a series of documents so that a criminal investigation on the former Labour grandee’s alleged leaks of sensitive information to the paedophile Jeffrey Epstein, who died in prison in 2019.

It is unclear what the new files will show or which part of his appointment they will relate to.

MPs on a security committee will now redact any information which may prejudice national security or international relations.

Documents in Epstein files at the beginning of the year appeared to show that Mandelson passed on confidential information about bailouts and Treasury assets to Epstein at around the time of the 2008 financial crisis.
