Chery’s new electric SUV is comfortable, roomy and loaded with kit, and it’s a close relative of the Jaecoo 7 that topped Britain’s sales chart in September. I drove a pre-production car in China, and if you want an EV with a name people will ask about in the company car park, it deserves a look, though the price will decide whether it deserves your money.

Lepas L6 EV price and UK launch date

The Lepas L6 EV is a comfortable, roomy electric family SUV with a long kit list and an official range of up to 279 miles, and on my drive it earned a place on any electric SUV shortlist. The steering is its weak spot, and the value case can’t be judged until Lepas names a price.

That price hasn’t been announced yet, but order books are due to open in the final quarter of this year, and dealers are already taking registrations of interest. The brand is on sale here already with the L8, a bigger plug-in hybrid SUV that costs £34,900 in Essence trim and £37,900 as an Elevate, which shows where Lepas is pitching itself. Motorpoint expects the L6 to start at around £30,000 to £32,000.

I drove a pre-production L6 EV over several days between Shanghai and Chery’s headquarters in Wuhu. It impressed me with its comfort and straightforward performance, although the steering felt artificial.

The L6 shares its technology with the Jaecoo 7, Chery’s plug-in hybrid SUV that was the UK’s best-selling car in September, and it joins Chery, Omoda, Jaecoo and the L8 in the company’s push into Britain. Its electric rivals include the Skoda Elroq, Kia EV3 and Volkswagen ID.4.

Who makes Lepas, and why does it exist?

Lepas is Chery’s newest brand, launched in April 2025. At the 2026 Chery International User Summit in Wuhu, which was the other reason I was in China, I asked Zhong Wei, Lepas’s deputy chief executive, why the world needed it.

For Mr Zhong, the brand reflects a shift in what buyers want. As people become more discerning, he says, they look for a car that expresses their personality and taste as well as getting them from A to B. Chery’s existing brands can’t satisfy every customer in the same way, he explained, so the company created a marque with its own identity, built around what he calls an elegant lifestyle of new-energy vehicles, intelligent technology and a more considered ownership experience.

That’s a big ask in Britain, where plenty of company-car drivers and private buyers have stuck with European badges for years. They’ll want to know what a Lepas is worth after three years, and because the brand is so new here, there’s no track record to tell them.

What is the Lepas L6 EV like to drive?

I drove the L6 EV on multi-lane expressways, across the flat roads of the Yangtze River Delta and along more scenic mountain routes.

It felt comfortable throughout, and acceleration was strong enough to make overtaking straightforward without the abrupt surge some electric cars produce. It also stayed composed on faster roads, in rain or shine (the part of China we were in seemed to deliver four seasons in one day). The cabin had enough room for four of us and our luggage, so it made a relaxed family car.

The L6’s main weakness is its steering, which lacks the feedback you get from some European brands. If all you want is a comfortable, easy SUV, you’ll barely notice, but if you enjoy a more connected drive, it’s the part of the L6 most likely to disappoint.

These impressions are based on a pre-production car, so the finished UK version may have different suspension and steering settings.

Lepas L6 EV range and charging

The L6 pairs a 65kWh battery with an electric motor producing 217PS and 275Nm of torque. Lepas quotes a 0 to 62mph time of 7.9 seconds and an official WLTP range of up to 279 miles.

Driving in China isn’t always easy, especially in downpours (it’s almost as tricky as London), so I kept my eyes on the road rather than the instruments for much of the trip. We covered 360km (223 miles) in a day on fairly fast expressways, in humid weather with the air-con running the whole time, and the range never became a worry.

Efficiency on that route hovered around 3.5 miles per kWh. That works out at roughly 225 miles from a full battery, about 50 miles short of the official figure, which is a fair result for fast driving in the heat with the air-con on, and it should cover most commutes for several days between charges.

Maximum DC charging power is 120kW, and Lepas says a 30 to 80 per cent top-up takes about 22 minutes. How the L6 copes with a British winter and UK chargers is something I’ll find out on the UK-spec drive.

Lepas L6 EV interior, boot space and technology

The dashboard has a 13.2-inch touchscreen and an 8.88-inch digital driver’s display, and the system is quick and easy to use. There’s also a Hello Lepas voice assistant, which I didn’t try because I don’t speak Chinese. The cameras are crystal clear, making parking a doddle even when you’re jetlagged in the middle of a Chinese service station, and I think they’d earn their keep in tight city streets and underground car parks, especially in London.

There are only two trims, Essence and Elevate. Both get 19-inch alloy wheels, a panoramic sunroof, a heated steering wheel and windscreen, 50W wireless phone charging, a 540-degree camera system, 22 driver-assistance functions and a 3.3kW vehicle-to-load socket. The Elevate adds heated and ventilated, electrically adjustable front seats, leather-effect upholstery, a power tailgate, an eight-speaker Sony stereo and parking assistance that includes remote parking. My pre-production car seemed to mix equipment from both, with fabric seats in place of the Elevate’s leather-effect finish.

We drove four-up for most of the trip, and there’s room for three across the back seat. All our luggage went into the 410-litre boot, which grows to 1,334 litres with the rear seats folded (we didn’t need to try that), and a 99-litre compartment under the floor is handy for charging cables or a work laptop you’d rather keep out of sight.

Lepas L6 EV company car tax and running costs

For company-car drivers, the L6 sits on the same 4 per cent benefit-in-kind rate as any electric car in the 2026/27 tax year, rising to 5 per cent from April 2027. If it were priced at £35,000, in line with the L8, that would be roughly £560 a year in tax for a 40 per cent taxpayer and £280 for a basic-rate one.

Private buyers will want to see the price before judging value, but the warranty is reassuring, with seven years or 100,000 miles on the car and eight years or 100,000 miles on the battery. RAC roadside cover comes free for the first year and can be renewed for up to seven years if you service the car at a Lepas dealer.

Is the Lepas L6 EV worth buying?

The L6 EV has the makings of a credible electric family SUV, with useful performance, a practical cabin and a long list of standard kit. The big unanswered question is value.

What we like

  • A claimed range of up to 279 miles, and about 225 miles in hot, fast real-world driving.
  • Comfortable cruising and plenty of room for a family and its luggage.
  • A long list of standard technology, including a 540-degree camera system that makes parking easy.

What worries us

  • Steering that felt artificial.
  • No confirmed UK price.
  • Unknown resale values for a brand that’s new to Britain.

If the L6 is on your list for when orders open, find out what your current car is worth with Regit’s free valuation, so you know how much a part-exchange could knock off the price.

Verdict

The Lepas L6 EV deserves a place on your electric SUV shortlist, because it’s comfortable and spacious, has a boot you wouldn’t turn your nose up at, and comes with a camera system that takes the stress out of tight streets and underground car parks. The steering needs work, though, and the L6 still has to prove itself on British roads.

Until Lepas confirms UK pricing, the value case is a blank, and with the L8 already at £34,900 the L6 needs to come in well below that. Get the number right and it could be a serious alternative to better-known electric SUVs such as the Skoda Elroq. I’ll be driving a UK-spec car in the coming weeks, and I’ll update this review when I have.

Whoever bought a BMW i7 new three years ago has watched well over half its price disappear, which is rotten luck for them and a gift for anyone shopping second-hand. Better still, a luxury EV registered before April 2025 escapes a tax that a new one pays for five years.

If you’ve ever fancied a BMW i7, the used market has made it a lot more realistic. Three-year-old cars are listed at dealers from about £45,000, according to AutoUncle listings we checked on 5 November, while the cheapest new i7 costs £104,230. Figures Auto Express published on 29 October show it’s part of a pattern, because the i7, Porsche Taycan, BMW i5, Audi e-tron GT and Mercedes EQS and EQE are all expected to be worth less than a third of their price new after three years and 36,000 miles.

Those Auto Express numbers are forecasts of what a car bought new today will fetch in part-exchange, set against its average list price, or the price of one version where it names one. Dealers ask more than part-exchange value, and plenty of these cars were sold with hefty discounts, so not every first owner has lost quite this much, but the size of the drop shows you where the bargains are.

Which luxury EVs lose the most value

1. Porsche Taycan

Average price new £162,255, expected value after three years about £50,475, so it’s expected to lose about £111,780.

No electric car in Auto Express’s figures loses more cash, though the average is dragged up by Turbo S and Turbo GT versions costing well over £150,000, and 2023 cars are listed from about £51,000. A 2023 car is the version before the 2024 update, which Porsche says brought up to 35% more range, so look up the official range for the exact car you’re looking at rather than going by a new one’s brochure.

2. BMW i7

Average price new £143,530, expected value after three years about £46,050, so it’s expected to lose about £97,480.

AutoUncle showed 21 three-year-old i7s for sale on 5 November, from £43,998, with most between about £47,000 and £63,000. Auto Express reckons the i7 is the wiser used buy of the two big electric limousines, ahead of the Mercedes EQS. Our motoring reporter Tim Barnes-Clay reviewed the facelifted 2026 i7, and two of the changes he found matter if you’re buying an older one. The update lifted BMW’s range figure to as much as 452 miles from 388, so a 2023 car won’t go as far on a charge, but it also took away the iDrive rotary controller, which Tim missed and which a 2023 car still has.

3. BMW i5

Average price new £110,045, expected value after three years about £34,650, so it’s expected to lose about £75,395.

The i5 is the electric 5 Series, long the default choice in the executive car park. Auto Express’s average is higher than the list price of even the top i5 M60 Touring (£98,425), so treat the cash figure as rough, but keeping about 31% of its value is the number that matters. It only went on sale in late 2023, so used ones are mostly 2024 cars or newer, and that’s fine for tax, because what counts is the date the car was first registered.

4. Audi e-tron GT

Price new £107,875 for the S e-tron GT, expected value after three years about £33,150, so it’s expected to lose about £74,725.

The e-tron GT shares its underpinnings with the Taycan, so it’s the closest thing to a Porsche with four rings on the bonnet. Auto Express’s figures are for today’s S e-tron GT, while 2023 cars are the earlier e-tron GT quattro, and used ones are thinner on the ground. One we found, a December 2023 car with about 13,700 miles, was up for £46,850, which AutoUncle reckons is about £5,000 more than it’s worth.

5. Mercedes EQS

Price new £104,540 for the EQS 450+ Premium, expected value after three years about £32,375, so it’s expected to lose about £72,165.

The EQS gives you S-Class space and quiet without an engine, and 2023 EQS 450+ saloons were listed from about £41,500 on 5 November. Auto Express isn’t a fan, though, and says rivals including the i7 are simply better all-round packages.

6. Mercedes EQE

Price new £86,615 for the EQE 350+ AMG Line Night Edition, expected value after three years about £26,850, so it’s expected to lose about £59,765.

The EQE is the smaller EQS, roughly an electric E-Class, and it’s the cheapest way into this club. AutoUncle had 29 three-year-old EQE 300s for sale on 5 November, between about £29,000 and £37,000, which is about what a new Volkswagen Golf costs. Cheaper electric cars lose even more in percentage terms, led by the Lexus UX 300e, and we’ve rounded those up separately.

Why a used luxury EV is cheaper to tax

What matters is the date on the log book. GOV.UK’s vehicle tax rate tables say any electric car first registered before 1 April 2025 never pays the £440 Expensive Car Supplement, however much it cost new, so it pays the £200 standard rate. Electric cars registered since then pay £10 in their first year, then £640 a year for the next five if their list price was over £50,000, which covers every car on this list.

That’s £2,200 over five years that a car registered before April 2025 never pays. October’s Budget raises the standard rate to £210 from April 2027, but the gap stays, and our guide to this year’s car tax changes covers the rest of the rates. Check the first registration date on the V5C before you buy, because an i5 registered in March 2025 and one registered in April look the same on the forecourt but don’t cost the same to tax.

In London, any electric car is ULEZ-free, and the Congestion Charge is £13.50 a day rather than £18 as long as the car is registered for Auto Pay, while plug-in hybrids pay the full £18. That matters if you want a 7 Series, because in 2023 BMW UK sold it only as the electric i7 or as a plug-in hybrid such as the 750e. Drive a 2023 750e into the zone on about 230 working days a year and the charge comes to £4,140, against £3,105 in an i7, so the i7 saves £1,035. Add the £440 supplement the 750e pays until its sixth year on the road and the i7 comes out almost £1,500 a year ahead. From April 2028, though, electric cars will also pay 3p a mile on top of road tax, which is about £270 a year if you cover 9,000 miles, and Regit has worked out what pay-per-mile tax will cost you at other mileages.

What to check before you buy

A 2023 car will only just have had its first MOT, so the service history tells you more than the MOT record. Ask for a battery health report, which shows how much of the original capacity is left, and check how long the battery warranty has to run. Make sure both charging cables come with the car, look at the tyres (heavy EVs get through them quickly) and get an insurance quote before you fall for one, because a car that’s cheap to buy is still expensive to insure.

When you’ve found the one, put its number plate into Regit’s free car valuation and you’ll know whether the dealer’s price for that i7 or EQS is fair before you start haggling.

Our verdict

Let someone else pay for the first three years. A 2023 BMW i7 from about £45,000 is our pick, because it has a back seat built for being driven around in, keeps the rotary controller the new one has lost and costs £200 a year to tax. If you’d rather drive than be driven, the Taycan from about £51,000 is the more exciting car, and the EQE from £29,000 is the cheapest way in, but whichever you choose, get the battery checked and the insurance quoted before you sign.

Mortgage holders are bracing for a “painful rise” in payments after the Bank of England tightened monetary policy for the first time since mid-2023.

The Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee raised interest rates to four per cent in a bid to stop inflation spiralling out of control amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. 

But the decision will cause a further squeeze on home owners, who are already struggling against rising bills, as higher borrowing drives up mortgage costs.

Around 2.3m households are due to come off fixed rate deals by the end of 2027, and could face higher bills when it comes to remortgaging. 

The majority of borrowers secured deals during periods of low rates, meaning they could see monthly repayments rise by hundreds of pounds.

Polling from City AM/ Freshwater Strategy, found 29 per cent of people believed they would be unable to afford the rise in bills off the back of the rise in mortgage bills.

According to Moneyfacts, the average two-year fixed mortgage rate stood at 5.87 per cent at the beginning of November. The average five-year fix was at six per cent.

Fixed mortgage rates are largely influenced by financial markets’ expectations of future interest rates and don’t reflect immediate shifts in the base rate. But the hawkish split of Monetary Policy Committee members, who all voted for a hike, may push fixed rates up as lenders price in the prospect of a higher rate regime.

“For mortgage holders, today’s decision will add to the pressure on household finances, particularly…those approaching the end of a fixed rate deal,” said Alexandra Loydon, group advice director at St James’s Place.

“With household budgets already stretched, even a small increase in monthly repayments could add to financial pressures.”

Tracker mortgage woes

The small number of households that are on tracker mortgages can expect a near-immediate rise in repayments. The products follow the fluctuation of the Bank’s central rate.

Tracker mortgage holders can expect a £30.72 monthly increase to their mortgage repayments, according to UK Finance.

Financial advisers said that while the sharp rise can be painful in the short term, those willing to hold on until rates come down again could secure a better deal in the long run.

Samuel Mather Holgate, managing director of advice firm Mather & Murray Financial, said: “For borrowers who can tolerate some uncertainty, a tracker mortgage could prove considerably better value, particularly if inflation pressures ease.”

But, David Hollingworth, associate director of L&C Mortgages, said there is “no guarantee that rates don’t keep on climbing”, warning people to only take on a tracker mortgage if they can handle the financial uncertainty.

Variable deals

Meanwhile, those on a standard variable rate (SVR), where the rate is set at the discretion of the lender, could also face higher repayments.

John Fraser-Tucker, head of mortgages at Mojo Mortgages, warned that letting your mortgage roll onto a SVR could “easily be the most expensive mistake a borrower could make right now”.

Roughly, 470,000 deals are on SVR, and if a lender decides to pass on the 0.25 percentage point increase in full, the average homeowner will see their monthly repayments increase by £14.28.

“The rate rise is likely to mean people with variable rate mortgages see another painful rise in their outgoings, so will need to find savings elsewhere,” said Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at AJ Bell.

“This is easier said than done, because prices have already been climbing, particularly at the pumps, and life is set to get harder in January, when a horrible hike in energy prices turns the screw on people’s budgets.”

Home to matcha bars, padel courts and beach clubs, Canggu is the poster child for Bali’s digital nomad transformation, but overtourism has seen some ward visitors away from the area. Anna Moloney checked into Hotel Tugu, the first hotel opened in Canggu, and The Regent, the coastline’s new, five-star luxury resort, to see how the area is still changing

In Robert Frost’s well known poem The Road Not Taken, it is “the path less traveled” that is upheld as the superior choice for its speaker. “Two roads diverged in a wood, and I—I took the one less traveled by, And that has made all the difference.”

I can only imagine, then, the contempt with which Mr Frost would regard my decision  to holiday in Bali – the road very much well travelled by, especially by well-to-do westerners just like myself.

Indeed, the island is now so popular (the annual number of international visitors has climbed 173 per cent in the last decade, clocking in at just under 7m in 2025) that its previous evangelists (who visited on gap yahs 10 years ago and told us all how fabulous it was) are quickly distancing themselves, shrieking things like “Bali is dead!” as they hurry off to Borneo.

Within Bali itself though, we can narrow the road most travelled even further, with that most trampled path of all leading straight from Denpasar airport to Canggu. 

Located on the southwestern coast, Canggu, a once sleepy fisherman’s village, has become the island’s digital nomad HQ, overflowing with matcha bars, luxury villas and beach clubs. You may recognise it from Instagram, where ‘Bali reality versus expectations’ videos frequently showcase ‘nightmare scenes’ of thousands of tourists packed cheek to cheek at popular sunset spots. Alongside the wellness scene, and similarly to the Thai islands, some clubs are open eye-wateringly late, attracting young, twenty-something crowds intent on ‘finding themselves’ amid seas of neon body paint. And while it may only be 12 miles from the airport, but journey times can stretch anywhere between 45 minutes to over two hours due to the region’s infamous traffic, with the village’s small roads often left in gridlock.

Indeed, the consensus of almost all good online advice on how to “do Bali well” in 2026 is to avoid Canggu, so that’s where I went first. Alas, popularity has never been something to put me off a holiday (I hold the inane belief that popular things are popular because they are nice), and if you want to understand how dramatically the island has changed just in the last couple of decades, there is no better place to start. 

Tugu: The first hotel in Canggu

The development of Canggu has been swift, and unanticipated. 

The first ever hotel in the area, the now five-star Hotel Tugu Bali, where I checked in, was opened in 1997 by Anhar Setjadibrata, a former Indonesian medical student who was taken by the beauty of Canggu, then just rice paddies, temples and the white sand beach. Today it’s managed by his daughter, Lucienne Anhar, who told me they could never have expected Canggu to become what it is today.

“Almost overnight, it switched,” she told me, pinpointing the moment to somewhere around 2015. The people who have come have also changed, shifting from honeymooners and hippy surfers to those interested in what Lucienne calls the ‘new Canggu’ – great restaurants, cafes, padel and gyms: “I think there are more restaurants and cafes per m2 in Canggu than even NYC.”

Tugu though is decisively of the old Canggu, steeped in history not only as the area’s original guesthouse but in a literal sense too, as a self-defined ‘museum hotel’. Duly, around the hotel you’ll find genuine Indonesian artefacts collected by Lucienne’s father, who opened Tugu partially as a way of storing and exhibiting his pieces, from rare portraits of Indonesian royals to Ming vases rescued from historical shipwrecks. Even the main lobby, a massive wooden pagoda supported by at least a dozen pillars surrounding a towering statue of the Hindu god Garuda, is a 150-year-old sacred ceremonial hall transported from a village in central Bali, which makes for a striking hangout spot amongst the rows of new built, laptop-friendly cafes. The guest lodgings themselves take the form of wooden villas built in a traditional Javanese style, strung together by planked footpaths hung over lotus ponds. 

The hospitality is traditional too, by which I mean very, very good. When I checked in and realised I had booked my room for the wrong date (completely my fault), they changed my reservation fuss-free on the spot, and promptly moved on to press rice grains onto my forehead by way of a welcome blessing. They also offer a unique service in that you can have breakfast wherever you want on the property, with the Tugu staff happy to set up a table in your room, the main lobby, or along one of the garden pathways.

Just steps from the beach, Tugu also represents prime real estate, and Lucienne confirmed that many have tried to buy it to put “another high rise building there”. ‘High-rise’ in this case admittedly means only a few storeys though, with Canggu still strictly regulated by the island’s 50-year-old ‘coconut tree’ rule, which prohibits buildings from exceeding 15 metres in height.

The Regent Bali: The new rich kid on the block

Notably, while I was visiting, Tugu had recently acquired one such ‘high rise’ (four-storey) neighbour in the form of Regent Bali Canggu, a new mega luxury, five-star resort which is now the biggest hotel in Canggu. With room rates over double that of Tugu, it’s a unique arrival for the area both in scale and price point, signalling a departure from the affordable luxury (cheap massages, acai bowls) that has traditionally drawn tourists to the area. Lucienne said she welcomed the arrival, which she hopes will “elevate” Canggu’s image to something more “upscale”, a new, new Canggu perhaps moving on from its digi nomad residents, who some locals told me are already mass migrating to Lombok and Uluwatu.

Indeed, staying at the Regent next, I could almost feel my nose starting to tip upwards as I was immediately swept up in golf carts and warm towels.

It’s a resort that’s been a long time in the making, with planning starting around 2010, potentially crucial to its financial viability: according to Asia-based hospitality consultant Matt Gebbie who has led research into the Bali tourism boom, in Canggu “if you haven’t owned the land for a generation, you are too late”, with rates finally catching up to more accurately reflect the high quality product on offer. “Luxury offerings in Bali are now earning the rates they deserve.”

Duly, the Regent is plush and beautiful. It’s been thoughtfully designed in a kind of stacked formation that progresses downhill to the beach. If you stand at the top and look down your eyes will follow a beautiful symmetry of layered pools, lined with palm trees, that culminate in the sea crashing at the bottom. The sea in Canggu is not particularly suitable for swimming, so this prime pool real estate is a particular luxury of the resort.

So too is the spa. You can’t go to Bali without getting a massage but my one at the Regent was among the most memorable, taking place on a warm sand bed that tipped forward and back as you lay on it – slightly unsettling but you soon learn to trust the grip of the sand. The spa complex itself is thoughtfully designed to incorporate outside hanging wicker meditation pods. For me, the addition of Dyson hairdryers with diffusers (a rarity any fellow curly-haired travellers will know the gift of) particularly impressed.

Cure is the resort’s fine dining option, and you can watch the sunset over the beach as you enjoy the delicious nectar of chef Andrew Walsh, whose original Cure restaurant in Singapore was awarded a Michelin star. The food is inspired by Asian and European flavours, not least from Walsh’s Irish heritage, and I particularly enjoyed the absurdity of chomping down on Irish potato bread (brown-sugar crushed and dipped in a bacon and spring onion emulsion) while watching the Indonesian sun set. 

A new, new Canggu

Is Canggu done? Hardly. Yes the traffic and crowds and constant construction noise are real problems – especially for locals – but to write off the entire area as a fad that has been done is as reductive as the original mania that crowned it an undiscovered paradise in the first place. Yes the traffic is bad, but that’s because lots of people want to go there (because it’s fun!) and it’s especially worth a couple nights if the majority of your trip is going to be in Bali’s more spiritual pockets. Instead, Canggu is evolving once again, and the arrival of the Regent marks an interesting addition of resort-scale luxury. 

Personally, as I waved goodbye to the Regent on departure, sipping on the iced coffee packed for me by the staff on checkout, I thought back to the Robert Frost poem: if this is the path well travelled, god don’t take me off it. 

Rooms at Hotel Tugu Bali start from around £153 per night.

Rooms at Regent Bali Canggu start from £369 per night.

The Bank of England has raised interest rates to four per cent as all policymakers agreed to tighten monetary policy in a bid to stop inflation from spiralling in the next year. 

The Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee hiked interest rates for the first time since mid-2023, with policymakers warning another hike could come in upcoming meetings. One rate-setter, Catherine Mann, voted to raise interest rates by 50 basis points in order to maintain credibility. 

The country’s most senior group of economists agreed that inflation could hit 4.9 per cent in the middle of next year. 

Governor Andrew Bailey indicated that today’s hike may not be the last amid concerns that a long war in the Middle East between the US and Iran could push prices higher.

“There is now enough inflationary pressure in the pipeline caused by the rise in energy prices, that an increase is warranted,” Bailey said. 

“Today’s increase shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. But, unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase”. 

Inflation spike forces Bank to act 

An acceleration in price growth over the next year would leave the Bank further away from its two per cent inflation target. 

The Bank’s main forecast suggests that inflation will only fall back to the target rate in late 2028. 

In the worst case that oil prices were above $100 (£74.3) per barrel for the next two years, inflation could hit 6.2 per cent while further interest rate hikes would be more likely. 

Rate-setters were more optimistic about the outlook for growth than several other forecasters, predicting that the UK economy would grow by 1.6 per cent this year and 1.3 per cent next year. However, the policy report warned that expected tax hikes kicking in from 2027 would weaken output. 

But Bailey told reporters that the UK’s growth “was not broad based”, and was instead largely down to white-collar industries’ rapid adoption of artificial intelligence.

“Just under a fifth of GDP [gross domestic product] growth this year has been accounted for by AI related activity,” he said, adding that policymakers were seeing an uptick in investment and usage.

“That doesn’t seem to me all that is surprising to the extent that there’s also an AI story in there,” Bailey said. “I think the first thing you’d expect to see in terms of this general purpose technology cycles is what you might call capital deepening of the sort that will then hopefully then lead to broader based productivity growth.”

According to the Bank, measures related to energy prices in the Budget will not lower inflation next year by more than 0.3 percentage points next year. 

Bailey signals one further interest rate hike

Markets had predicted that at least one policymaker would vote for interest rates to be held. Alan Taylor, the MPC member who was seen as the most likely dissenter against a hike, referred to the latest decision as “insurance”. 

Bank members suggested that there was little evidence of second round effects in the UK economy, the event where higher inflation prompts workers to demand higher wages, pushing up price pressures across the country. 

But the MPC concluded there was “pressure in the pipeline” as higher costs were set to feed into the price of goods around the world. Bailey said one further hike was on the horizon if inflationary pressures did not immediately ease. 

Since the US mid-terms, oil prices have fallen by more than seven per cent as President Trump is facing considerable pressure to bring his war with Iran to a close. The Bank’s forecast did not take account of the latest market pricing, with judgements made based on data up until late October. 

The main report also warned that, as a result of higher interest rate expectations, annual average mortgage payments are likely to be about £1,500 higher by the 2029 than had been predicted before the war in the Middle East.

Microsoft has opted against expanding a major data centre deal with British AI dealing Nscale that could have been worth tens of billions of dollars, in fresh sign of the challenges facing the industry’s vast infrastructure spending plans.

The US tech giant decided not to take up an option to more than double the computing capacity it rents from the Nvidia-backed company at a site in Texas.

However, the decision was made several months ago, a source familiar with the matter said, before its September stock market filing. They stressed that its existing contracts with Microsoft remained unaffected.

The London-headquartered firm, which counts former deputy prime minister Nick Clegg and former Meta executive Sheryl Sandberg among its board members, has become one of Britain’s most valuable AI start-ups by securing multibillion-dollar contracts to supply the computing power needed to run artificial intelligence.

City AM understands that the data centre firm’s existing Ward Country contract with Microsoft remains unaffected.

The decision follows Microsoft’s withdrawal last month from a separate Nscale data centre project in Essex, although the British firm insisted its wider relationship with the US tech giant remained strong.

Under an agreement struck in October last year, Microsoft committed to renting around 240 megawatts of computing capacity at Nscale’s Ward County development in Texas, with the option to take significantly more.

Another Microsoft setback

That additional capacity, equivalent to roughly 500 megawatts, could have generated tens of billions of dollars in future revenue for Nscale.

Microsoft has decided against taking up the option. The existing agreement remains intact, while Nscale is understood to be in discussions with other potential customers for the available capacity.

The decision does not affect its reported $103bn (£76.5bn) backlog of contracted future business. Although it does remove a potentially lucrative source of additional revenue.

The company operates a data centre on land leased from cryptocurrency miner Ionic Digital in Ward County, where it has built the infrastructure needed to supply Microsoft.

It is also developing a neighbouring site on land it owns, where robotics company Figure AI has signed up as a customer.

“Our owned site in Ward County is already being built to serve Figure AI and other AI natives and we’re already in discussions with several major customers for the rest of that capacity,” Nscale said.

The two developments form part of Nscale’s wider plans for up to 1.2 gigawatts of computing capacity in Ward County.

The company added that its relationship with Microsoft remained in good standing, with work continuing on contracted projects in Norway, Portugal and Texas.

AI spending hits bottleneck

It follows Microsoft’s withdrawal last month from Nscale’s flagship UK data centre project in Loughton, Essex, which had been championed by the government as a cornerstone of Britain’s AI ambitions.

The £2bn development was originally expected to open next year but has been hit by delays securing enough electricity to power the site.

UK Power Networks has reportedly indicated that sufficient grid capacity may not be available until the early to mid-2030s, leaving Nscale exploring alternative power sources.

Microsoft, which had been expected to become the site’s main customer, pulled out of the arrangement but maintained that it remained committed to its wider partnership with Nscale.

The decisions come as investors increasingly scrutinise the enormous sums being committed to AI infrastructure, particularly by companies borrowing heavily to build data centres before they become operational.

Nscale is targeting a valuation of as much as $35bn in its planned New York listing, over double the roughly $14.6bn valuation it secured in a funding round earlier this year.

Nscale secures deal with Anthropic

The company, founded by former cryptocurrency miner Josh Payne, reported a $1bn net loss on revenue of just $141m in the first half of 2026, with much of the loss attributed to non-cash charges.

Its business model relies on securing long-term contracts with major tech giants before raising the vast sums needed to build and equip data centres.

That makes commitments from customers like Microsoft and Anthropic particularly important. Investors are increasingly scrutinising whether the enormous sums being poured into AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.

Nscale has already secured a deal worth around $45bn to supply Anthropic with computing power from its West Virginia campus and is reportedly negotiating a second agreement of similar size.

However, that project has also faced construction delays and local opposition, adding to the challenges facing the company’s rapid expansion.

Comments from members of the Bank of England’s rate-setting committee suggest more interest rate hikes are on the way, writes Mauricio Alencar.

‘Stands to ready to act’ was the Bank of England’s mantra for most of this year as it waited for higher energy prices to trickle through the UK economy. After today, the Monetary Policy Committee is no longer standing still. 

Bank officials surprised City analysts by voting in unison to raise rates. Forecasters had predicted splits in the committee and a ‘on-the-fence’ approach to signalling further hikes. 

Instead, the only dissent that came was in Catherine Mann’s decision to vote for interest rates to rise by 50 basis points to 4.25 per cent. And Governor Andrew Bailey appears to be leading the charge for at least one further hike.

Explaining his decision, the Bank governor said that “without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates”. It makes it clear that the Bank looks poised to raise borrowing costs further unless a miracle takes place and price pressures simmer out. 

Megan Greene, Sarah Breeden, Huw Pill and Clare Lombardelli were the other members of the nine-strong committee to say a further hike appeared to be on the horizon. Their views were in stark contrast to external member Alan Taylor, who suggested today’s decision was a ‘one-and-done’. Not everyone on the MPC thinks the same. 

The Bank is leaning on “pressure in the pipeline” rather than evidence of real-time effects. While fuel and household energy costs are set to be much higher than economists would have wished, policymakers noted there was still little evidence of price effects spiralling out of control. 

It is taking a firm judgment call that business will pass on higher costs onto consumers in the coming months, which could trigger a violent reaction in price-setting and wage-bargaining among households and firms. Inflation is now set to peak at about 1.5 percentage points higher than it had previously forecast in July. Price growth will hit 4.9 per cent next summer, according to central forecasts.

Ultimately — like Chancellor John Healey — governor Andrew Bailey is a hostage to Donald Trump. While oil and gas prices have fallen after a crushing mid-terms verdict of the US president’s war in Iran, markets still maintained exepctations of multiple interest rate hikes taking place. 

By indirect means, Bailey issued a plea for Trump to end the war, saying interest rates would have to rise “unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved”. City traders were, after all, not wrong to factor in the risk of several hikes. The Bank has now responded to markets but will decide to enter a rate-hiking cycle?

Wild Izakaya review and star rating: ★★★★

The first thing you notice about Wild Izakaya is that this restaurant definitely used to be an office. Just what you want if you’ve just spent all day in yours. Dinner’s served with an evening dose of industrial-chic and polished concrete flooring!

Warming the space is a busy, open, central kitchen, from which steam billows high into those corporate rafters. Weirdly, my first thought is that Wild Izakaya reminds me of Scott’s, its frontage refusing to give away any of the restaurant’s secrets. An unassuming doorway leads to a dining room that manages to be simultaneously cosy, chaotic and theatrical. On a Monday evening, it was heaving.

Wild Izakaya: sushi in the City

There isn’t enough of this sort of thing in the City. We’re big fans of Luma Omakase’s cosmic sushi counter, and for a quick lunch there’s Koya in Bloomberg Arcade, while there’s always bridge-and-tunnel favourite – and Toast the City Award winner – Sushisamba if you want to get squiffy while eating your sushi to the accompaniment of live DJs. But in purely culinary terms, the Square Mile is under-represented when it comes to raw sliced fish.

Wild Izakaya helps to redress the balance. It was founded by George Bukhov-Weinstein and Ilya Demichev of the Wild Group, whose ten restaurants in London include Goodman, Lita in Marylebone and Wild in Notting Hill. This new venue – inspired by the Japanese izakaya pubs – is a bold new direction that extends their culinary repertoire beyond their Italian, US and Greek stalwarts. Executive chef Satoru Hashimoto arrives from Hokkaido via Koya in Mayfair, having spent more than a decade in Nobu Kitchens.

My advice is to forget whatever you think you know about sushi. Put your ego in the cupboard and eat whatever the staff say is good that day. Even if you do know a little about sushi (which, again, you probably don’t), feign ignorance – being led through the experience is part of the joy. Sit back and act like a spoiled prince, letting the good stuff be presented to you. The fatty tuna belly (which has the best flavour), the mackerel, the yellowtail, the turbot and the red sea bream – it all arrives fresh from Japan, air-shipped daily.

Dedicated sake specialist

There’s a dedicated sake specialist, too. Despite the odd brewery (there’s the very good Shogun Sakes in Peckham) sake is still underrepresented on these shores and largely misunderstood. Thankfully, recommendations are fast and fuss free. I particularly enjoyed a 17.5 per cent Nabeshima Daiginjo from the Saga region, as well as the painted sake urn etched with colourful drawings of sumo wrestlers, including matching cups.

The restaurant’s menu follows the familiar formula of nigiri and sashimi and maki rice rolls, followed by fried meat, skewers and fish. Start off restrained if you intend on surviving the five-course onslaught. With hindsight, the appetisers would probably make more sense as sides, but we behaved by ordering them first. We had the king crab cucumber salad, which was wonderfully minimalistic, and a punchy and colourful sashimi salad adorned with seaweed and a light ponzu dressing.

For the nigiri course we went conservative, enjoying wedges of salmon and tuna lopped off the animal a mere metre from our faces. We interrupted the chef with questions while we chomped. “Which one is that?” They must hate working out front, especially when they get someone like me seated in front of them. Next came fine slivers of scallop, vibrant enough they don’t need the bells and whistles of the cooked variants you find in gastropubs.

Jidori chicken

The WFC Karaage is the capital’s latest attempt at giving fried chicken a glow-up (another is the Claridge’s Fried Chicken) this fried Jidori chicken representing the menu’s first hit of hedonism after the cold courses.

From the skewers, the wagyu with shoyu koji is hella indulgent – the sticks decorated with great chunks of this famous cow, which urban legend would suggest are serenaded by classical musicians and massaged in their native Japan. The sake pourers diligently paired something new each time – saltier, sweeter, boozier, more refined – each serving arriving in an impossibly cute little cup.

You get the impression everyone genuinely gives a shit. The service is flawless and the recommendations on point – mostly, it’s just aggressively fun. Sit at the counter and lean in to the anything goes approach.

Go to wildizakaya.co.uk or call 020 8191 3261

In the wake of Donald Trump’s midterms misery, Andy Burnham should be careful not to mistake a lame duck for a tame one, writes Michael Martin

President Trump was never going to retire quietly, nor accept the blame for the Republicans’ midterm losses. As Democrats swept both chambers of Congress, his defence was that his name was not on the ballot. Candidates who spent months fighting uphill campaigns against historically high petrol prices, in a nation where nearly nine in 10 drive to work, will see it very differently.

Nevertheless, Tuesday’s result fired the starting gun on Trump’s lame-duck presidency. Having lost Congress, and with it the confidence of his party’s most motivated voters, he will find his authority tested soon. Vice-President JD Vance and secretary of state Marco Rubio will probably begin jostling to define post-Trump Republicanism. That will not sit well with a President obsessed with how others perceive his power and authority.

But No 10 should not confuse a lame duck with a tame one. A President stripped of domestic strength does not become less powerful, he simply has fewer places to exercise it. With a hostile Congress blocking him at home and no elections left to fight, Trump will turn to the one arena where the constitution still gives him a free hand: foreign policy. While his would-be successors build their brands for 2028, he will sprint to secure his legacy, most likely through a settlement in Ukraine and an end to the war with Iran, one way or another. He will pursue both with the undivided attention of a man with nothing left to lose. And his approach may come with fewer tariffs and sanctions and more from US troop moves and material withholding.

This week was a heavy defeat for Trump. Yet it also brings him a kind of freedom. He has no further campaigns to run, has never shown much inclination towards decorum, and will likely test his constitutional authority and the executive branch’s loyalty until the very last moment.

Could this be the most dangerous Trump for Burnham?

This is precisely when Britain’s exposure is greatest, which is why the Prime Minister’s response to the results was a misjudgement. Burnham read the American result as an endorsement of his own agenda, saying voters wanted an end to the war in Iran and a focus on the cost of living. As domestic politics, it makes sense. Anti-Trump sentiment runs deep, especially on the left, and with an early election possible, Burnham wants that vote consolidated. But there is a reason British Prime Ministers have traditionally avoided taking sides in American election results, because Britain must work with whoever occupies the White House.

The stakes have rarely been higher. For better or worse, the United States remains the guarantor of European and British security. Cyber-attacks on critical infrastructure are routine, coordinated bomb threats against civilian aircraft are becoming commonplace across Europe and our Baltic NATO allies face regular probing for weakness.

Some will argue that years of British deference, and two state visits, bought little. There is something in that. But the answer is national strength, which means a credible defence and intelligence budget, not a soundbite the morning after an election. Political capital spent scoring points against Trump buys applause at home, but costs support abroad.

Burnham can choose his words with care, as his work this week on an apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade showed. He should apply similar discipline now. Trump is weakened, not finished, and the next two years may be the most consequential, and dangerous, of his presidency for Britain. The national interest is served by putting it above party politics when it matters, however uncomfortable, not by racing to use the result for a point or two in the polls.

Michael Martins is the founder of Overton Advisory and formerly a staffer at the London US embassy

On this day, 5 November 1991, the body of Robert Maxwell was dredged up from the Atlantic Ocean. Eliot Wilson traces the rise and fall of the media tycoon

25 years ago, just after 6.00 pm on 5 November 1991, the body of a 68-year-old man was winched out of the Atlantic Ocean near Gran Canaria by a helicopter from the Spanish Air Force’s search-and-rescue division. The crew gave an immortal and pithy description of the 22-stone corpse: “desnudo, rígido y flotando”, naked, stiff and floating. The man had apparently drowned after falling from a yacht.

Robert Maxwell was a huge figure, in physical size and ego. He seemed invented, and was frequently compared to Augustus Melmotte, the villain of Anthony Trollope’s The Way We Live Now.

He was. Maxwell would turn out to be the epitome of a self-made man who worshipped his creator. That element of fiction, of deceit and misdirection, would run through his life like a thread of fool’s gold.

The early years

He was born on 10 June 1923 in Slatinské Doly, in the then-new state of Czechoslovakia. He was from a family of Yiddish-speaking Orthodox Jews: his father Mechel tried to register him as Abraham Lajbi Hoch, but the town hall clerk had told him he must choose Czech names. So Robert Maxwell first entered the record as Ján Ludvík Hyman Binjamin Hoch.

His parents were peasant labourers in the poorest part of Czechoslovakia, his father also serving as a shochet, a kosher butcher. But his mother wanted Ludvík, as her eldest son, to be a rabbi. He went first to a yeshiva, where he learned Yiddish, Hebrew and Czech, then to a state school where he added Russian, as well as German from his classmates.

By 13, he was juggling five languages, living in poverty unimaginable in Western Europe at that time, in a region of diversity and fragility: Ruthenians, Hungarians and Czechs lived alongside the Jewish community, with the Great Depression making life harder and the ever-present crackle of antisemitism always within earshot.

The hinge of Maxwell’s life was a four-day period, 15-18 March 1939. Nazi Germany annexed Czechoslovakia, but Germany’s ally Hungary collected a few scraps from the table. The Royal Hungarian Army occupied Subcarpathian Ruthenia, including Maxwell’s home town of Slatinské Doly, and a nightmare would slowly unfold.

Maxwell was 15, studying at the Pressburger Yeshiva in Bratislava. Hungary imposed increasingly stringent restrictions on Jews’ economic and public life. He had to get out so fled to Budapest then France, and finally to England. There were more new names, Ivan or Leslie du Maurier, when he joined the British Army.

He was lucky. Early in 1944, Hitler ordered the occupation of Hungary. In eight weeks, 437,000 Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau, and three-quarters were killed more or less on arrival. Maxwell’s pre-War life was essentially erased: his parents, his brother, three sisters, grandfather and more than 300 relatives were murdered. The Hoch family was gone.

Just 21, Maxwell served with the North Staffordshire Regiment from Normandy to Berlin, was promoted to sergeant, commissioned as an officer and received the Military Cross from Field Marshal Montgomery personally. After the War he stayed in Berlin for two years with the Foreign Office press section, was naturalised as a British subject and changed his name to Ian Robert Maxwell.

The creation of Robert Maxwell

The young man was created anew: Captain Robert Maxwell MC, tall, dashing, with a deep baritone voice and clipped, precise diction. He was an instinctive linguist, enterprising, persuasive and recklessly brave, decorated for storming a German machine gun position. That he was a work of his own art was not exceptional among the one in three European Jews who survived the Holocaust.

But Maxwell had a heart of darkness. By his early 20s, life had taught him critical lessons. He wanted enormous and conspicuous financial success, he wanted power, he wanted to be part of the Establishment (on his own terms) and he had a ruthless will to succeed. And he never wanted to be hungry.

Maxwell’s rise is a familiar story. He became the British and American distributor for specialist publisher Springer Verlag, then founded Butterworth-Springer, later Pergamon Press. He expanded it to a formidable scientific press, producing earnestly obscure papers and columns, and it gave him a platform of worthy respectability.

He became the Labour parliamentary candidate in Buckingham in 1959, having told the local party he was “of farm labouring stock [who], with only his army gratuity behind him, started a scientific publishing business”. Some of the words were true but missed his essence. He was elected in 1964 and held the marginal seat until 1970.

His energy and supposed familiarity with science chimed with Harold Wilson’s talk of technology, research and “the Britain that will be forged in the white heat of this revolution”. Yet ministerial office did not come and the backbenches of the House of Commons could not contain him. His zenith was as an efficiency-minded chairman of the Catering Committee: he sold off the House’s impressive cellar of vintage wine at knock-down prices, some bottles seeming to find their way into his own possession.

In 1969, Maxwell tried to buy The News of the World but was knocked back. He was also ejected from the board of Pergamon Press: a 1971 inquiry by the Department of Trade and Industry concluded he was not “a person who can be relied on to exercise proper stewardship of a publicly quoted company”.

Undeterred, he acquired Mirror Group Newspapers, publishers of The Daily Mirror and five other papers, in 1984. It was not yet an empire to rival that of his enemy Rupert Murdoch, but he had no intention of stopping there.

In 1987 he launched the short-lived The London Daily News. He had also acquired the Berlitz language schools, a half-share of MTV Europe and American publishers Macmillan Inc. In 1990, he launched an ambitious transnational newspaper, The European, attempting to capture the zeitgeist of the end of the Cold War. Then, in 1991, he bought into an ailing populist icon, The New York Daily News.

The beginning of the end

This eclectic empire was built on a flimsy pontoon of loans and theft, and it was beginning to sink. He was billions of pounds in debt, his private businesses owing around £1bn and Maxwell Communications Corporation anywhere between £1.4bn and £2bn. On top of that, it would transpire that he had been using assets belonging to his companies’ pension funds as collateral and shuffling funds between companies to maintain solvency. The futures of 32,000 members of various pension schemes were suddenly uncertain.

By October 1991, banks were demanding repayment or selling shares used as collateral. The end was coming. The night before he died, Maxwell had an argument by telephone with his son Kevin over a meeting with the Bank of England, concerning a default on a £50m loan. The unfurling saga of Maxwell’s financial chicanery, the theft of half a billion pounds from the pension funds, was grim.

Was Robert Maxwell a crook? Certainly. He had taken other people’s money to shore up his own position and left them in dire financial straits; even with substantial government assistance, pensioners only received half their entitlement. Was he a bully? Unquestionably. He tormented those over whom he had power, undermining their authority and bugging their telephone calls. He was also savagely litigious.

Essentially people were only important as allies or obstacles in his own rise. Everything was subjugated to his pursuit of success. His persona, as a fabulously wealthy tycoon, was only a veneer; it was a dinner jacket borrowed from a hire company. His rivalry with Rupert Murdoch (current fortune $25bn) was never really a match of equals. It had all been a lie.

Yet it had been a lie which many had chosen to believe. When he died, John Major and Neil Kinnock had paid tribute to him; Peter Jay and Alastair Campbell had worked for him and defended him. The circles in which he moved had accepted the word of a liar.

Are monsters born or made? Probably both. The pitiless harrowing of the Shoah may have killed any warmth in Jan Ludvík Hoch. After that his undoubted gifts and insatiable ambition drove him on, and there were many casualties. Perhaps it is in fact a trinity: monsters are born, made, and enabled.

Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian. He is a senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity and a contributing editor at Defence on the Brink

No one alive has worked in the City longer than David Buik. He tells Ali Lyon what’s changed since his first day in September 1962, and what, mercifully, has remained the same.

It is 12:30 on a mild Tuesday afternoon, and as he takes to his blue leather stool and peruses his paper menu, David Buik is exactly where he is meant to be.

The City grandee can’t recall the exact number of times he’s frequented Mansion House’s Sweetings restaurant, but the historic Victorian-era eatery – best known for its inviting, anachronistic menu and equally inviting, anachronistic interiors – is a lunch destination of which the financial veteran of 64 years heartily approves.

“There have been a lot of really great restaurants in the City over the years, but Sweetings is…” his voice trails off, and his face scrunches up into a grimace of approval. “It’s the best.”

Our choice of Square Mile haunt is also sound given the backstory of the man I am here to meet. Sweetings has endured, essentially unchanged, for nearly 140 years. It survived two world wars, six owners, and the erection and demolition of skyscrapers – not to mention the coming and going of their speculative occupants. And while Buik’s own City career, which spanned the worlds of money broking, derivatives broking, financial PR and media commentary, may not have quite stretched over a century, he has stalked the City’s cobbled streets for well over half of one.

From ‘abysmal’ A Levels to a career in the City

The 82-year-old secured his first job in the financial district – straight out of school after an “abysmal set of A Level results” – in 1962, and since that first gig as a bank clerk, has borne witness to each of the City’s booms and busts, developments and regressions, from a front-row seat. There was rampant inflation of the 1970s, the abolition of exchange controls in 1979 – the “biggest change of my entire career”, the 2008 financial crisis and – of course – Margaret Thatcher’s ‘Big Bang’, whose 40th anniversary was celebrated by many City folk of Buik’s vintage last week. And be it City Index, Prebon Yamane, Cantor Index or Panmure Gordon, Buik has also outlasted many of the institutions where he once plied his trade.

Now, over six decades since first stepping into the Moorgate office of Philip Hill, Higginson, Erlanger, Buik has chronicled his vast professional adventures in a book: Money Markets Mayhem.

“I am just one of those really fortunate people who, as a person of modest ability, had a wonderful job,” he says after being asked why he took on the Herculean task of documenting such a varied and storied career. “And I don’t know anybody else – I don’t think – who’s worked here for longer.”

The world that Buik first entered on 17 September 1962 was a galaxy away from the Mansion House that we are both looking out on over a glass of white burgundy. Now, in the large office across from us, there are poorly-attended desks with four monitors each and conference rooms boasting vast projectors for the day’s international video calls. There are professionals hurriedly marching to their pit-stop of choice, destined – heaven forbid – to return, paper bag in hand, to eat at their desk. And – to Buik’s evident dismay – there is not a single suit and tie to be seen.

By contrast, on Buik’s first day at Philip Hill, Higginson, Erlanger, his manager gave him his marching orders for having the temerity to turn up in a “pale-blue shirt, collar attached and a plain dark-blue tie”.

“The office manager – a fierce Scotsman who had lost a leg on the Somme in World War I, looked at me sternly over his spectacles and asked me, in a thick broad Glaswegian accent, whether I was in the habit of coming to work in my pyjamas,” he writes. “I was sent home to dress appropriately.”

‘What people miss in the City now is the fun’

The salaries are just a shade different, too. Buik’s first monthly paycheck was the princely sum of £39 17s 6d, which now, according to the Bank of England’s inflation checker, would be a smidge under £780 a month. And as opposed to the sorry-looking sandwiches or sushi which today’s execs are hurriedly scoffing, the then-trainee would take his 3s lunch voucher (15p in today’s money) to the Sterling Castle for a steak and kidney pudding, chips and half-pint of bitter.

Appropriately, given our setting, it is this last difference about which Buik appears most exercised. The long City lunch, he says, is a fine tradition that has gone back decades. It produces serendipitous conversations, cultivates relationships, and is both fruitful and – crucially – enjoyable. But it is also, my interviewee fears, endangered.

“I think what people miss now is the fun,” he says, a hearty fish pie immediately before him, and a sea of Pret baguettes and salads beyond the window outside. “I recently went to a Japanese restaurant in the West End with an old friend from Barclays, and was sitting on a table next door to a broker and hedge fund manager. Apart from saying hello to one another they barely exchanged a single word: they were just on their phones.

“I, on the other hand, was out to lunch at least three times a week, and would either go to the opera or ballet at least once.”

Aside from execs’ increasingly subsistent relationship with food, Buik’s other great bete noire of contemporary life is the predominance of technology. Over our hour-and-a-half-long conversation, he grabs my phone three times as a prop for anecdotes to which the device was a pejorative punchline, and he is concerned about the impact it will have on his grandchildren’s livelihoods. “The thing that worries me – or upsets me – more than anything else is what technology is doing. These damned things – it’s an epidemic.”

But to paint Buik as a nostalgic luddite would be to do a disservice to a man whose nuanced, acerbic financial insights made him one of the most recognised financial commentators of any generation. Regular turns on the BBC, LBC and in newspapers including this one helped boost his and the City’s profile – eventually earning him an MBE for services to finance. And his unashamedly pro-enterprise worldview has even helped him amass more than 55,000 followers on the very social media platforms about which he has so many misgivings.

To the veteran, there are many areas in which the Square Mile is just as good or indeed better than the early stages of his career. “It’s less closed off and cosseted than it was, which is certainly a good thing. And in the world of derivatives, foreign exchange, insurance, professional services, we’re still number one.”

‘My number one passion is people’

That pride is part of the reason why Buik chose to put pen to paper on his memoir. For all its financial and cultural heft, the City is not, he says, given the credit it deserves in the wider firmament: something which he hopes, by steering clear of “sex and drugs” or “greed and excess” to correct.

“I’m so tired of hearing people vilifying the City, slagging it off, and giving it a really hard time. We need to consider that – together with the rest of the financial sector – it contributes £100bn to the Exchequer. And I just find it irritating that people don’t.”

The book offers no shortage of characteristically eccentric anecdotes, too. There’s the one where, during a stint in Tokyo, he could not understand why, despite lathering himself in aftershave, the locals avoided sitting next to him on the tube. A colleague duly informed him that he – like every western visitor – smelled of dairy and was thus unobliging company on a jam-packed tube. And there’s the time when, ahead of asking the parents of his first wife for their permission to marry her, he indulged in a six-bottle lunch with a colleague – only to fall asleep in an ice-cold bath to be woken up at 9pm by a call from his affianced, asking where he was. “Ali, I was smashed,” he remembers. “I could have died of hypothermia had that phone not gone off.”

But for all the fun memories, and the cheerleading and championing of what was his spiritual home for over six decades, Money Market Mayhem is, deep down, a book about people. Its 300 pages could act as a Who’s Who of the great, good, and some not so good, of British finance. Its castlist brims with household names like Robert Maxwell, Alastair Campbell and Lord Spencer, whom he describes as “by far” the biggest influence on his career. Graham Sounness – the former Liverpool player and manager – also crops up, as does the comedian Rory Bremner,  who is quoted on the book sleeve and who, Buik says, does a “wicked” impersonation of his unapologetic received pronunciation.

“I have four real loves in life: I love my career, I love horse racing, I love my family, but above all, I love people – it’s part of the reason I was such a lousy manager – I could never lay anyone off.”

The irrepressibly courteous Buik is on what must be his eighth “he’s just a lovely man” of the meal as he thanks our waitress profusely for the “delicious” fayre. And I am reminded of Buik’s tonic to life; one that helped him survive longer at the front line of UK finance than anyone else alive.

“I have always attached great credence to food,” he writes. “Good company, revelry, humour, gossip and great ‘craic’, supplemented with tasty food and above-average wine, go to make the greatest hobby of all time.”

I saunter off, immediately consulting my phone and anxious to return to my desk’s multi-screen set-up. And I leave Buik, and Sweetings, to remain exactly as they are.

Money Markets Mayhem, by David Buik, is out now and available on Amazon.

Kane’s €25m (£21m) per year deal maintains his status as the highest paid player in Germany’s Bundesliga and among a handful of elite earners in European football.

It comes after the prolific 33-year-old striker last week became the first Englishman to be awarded the Ballon d’Or for the world’s best player in 25 years.

Kane’s new contract is not reported to include an increase in basic salary but does come with an improved bonus structure that could boost his pay to as much as €33m (£27m).

Since joining from Tottenham Hotspur in 2023, he has scored 156 goals in 161 games and won five trophies, including two Bundesliga titles.

“What began as a major transfer has, over time, become a special chapter in FC Bayern’s history,” said club president Herbert Hainer.

Ed Warner on the deluge of work that is triggered by the end of cricket’s County Championship, from recruitment and sponsorship to strategic planning for a possible fall in media rights revenue.

The sun never sets on modern day cricket. Just ask the Australian squad, five matches into a 21-Test stretch across 12 months and under the cosh from both national media and past players. Fancy a swift cricket fix this weekend? There’s a clutch of matches in the Abu Dhabi T10 tournament that starts on Saturday. You’ll find them in the UK on Premier Sports.

I had thought that my first off-season as a county chair would be an opportunity to de-stress, but was swiftly disabused of the notion. If anything, the workload stepped up once stumps were pulled for the final time in the English summer (or more accurately, early autumn), and Sussex’s players scattered on holidays, international duty or overseas employment.

As a fan, the end of the domestic season is an opportunity for other sporting interests to crowd in. As an administrator, autumn is the season of hellos and goodbyes, recruitment interviews, sponsor and membership renewals, budgeting and strategic planning. It is as if a deluge of work has been held back by the activity of cricket itself. Only once that necessary focus on the sport is removed can preparations for the next season begin in earnest.

As has been well reported, including here, Sussex Cricket is operating under “special measures” imposed by the England and Wales Cricket Board as a result of past poor financial management and governance failings. While this has added to the list of essential tasks that are dominating our diaries right now, a trawl of specialist cricket media and announcements from other counties reveals that we are far from alone in having to reshape our leadership and playing roster. The merry-go-round of talent is spinning faster than ever, the money in global franchise cricket proving its accelerator.

Just this week we welcomed new men’s head coach Matt Walker to his first day of work at our County Ground. The first members of his squad will arrive back for fitness conditioning work in a couple of weeks. We were also delighted to announce the appointment of our new CEO, Beth Barrett-Wild, who has most recently spent 13 years at the ECB in leadership roles in women’s cricket, including as tournament director at this summer’s ICC Women’s T20 World Cup. The response to Beth from within cricket and sport more widely has been phenomenally positive. In between, we appointed five new directors, completing a refresh of the board that began earlier in the year.

“The opportunity to lead and help shape the future of the oldest professional cricket club in the world is something eight-year-old Beth could only have dreamt of.”

Beth Barrett-Wild on her appointment as Sussex Cricket CEO

In the next couple of days we will hopefully go public with the hiring of a new director of cricket. Next up after that, a couple of player signings and a high-profile former cricketer to be nominated to our members as Sussex Cricket’s next president.

All of this activity is taking place against the backdrop of movements elsewhere across the sport as well as rumours and misdirections. It may be that the growing propensity of many news outlets to report on overseas matches from UK sofas rather than sending correspondents abroad has increased the gossip quotient. Idle hands and minds and all that. Or, just as likely, editor demands for 24hr rolling updates. I confess it’s fun and frustrating in equal measure to be in the maelstrom.

The strategic planning at all first class counties, and the ECB itself as the sport’s national ruling body, is currently dominated by talk of the next round of TV rights deals, both here and internationally. The strong sense is that values will likely be flat at best, with a very real risk that they will be down. If so, the financial consequences would be felt throughout cricket.

The biggest single contributor to the ECB’s revenues is broadcast income. Remember, unlike the FA in football and the RFU in rugby, the ECB does not own its own ground and all the income opportunities that come with ownership of Wembley and Twickenham. If the Indian TV market softens on cricket, that’s less money for the International Cricket Council, and hence less to be distributed by it to the ECB. If Sky TV in turn were to bid less for domestic cricket rights, that’s less income again for the ECB.

Forget next year’s Ashes and all the talk of steep ticket prices, the only years in which the ECB turns a profit are when India play a Test series here. All down to TV revenue.

One link down the chain, payments from the ECB represent the biggest single element of Sussex’s income, as is the case for most of our county counterparts. You’ll appreciate, then, that there is an urgency about our search both for new commercial income and for different ways to monetise the use of our ground – after all, cricket is only played there around 50 times a year.

We need, too, to explore ways to inject fresh capital into our business while preserving the precious engagement with our members – both individuals and local clubs – who are our owners. Buy what is in effect a season ticket and you become an owner of Sussex Cricket, which is a fantastic protection for our heritage that stretches back to 1839, but can also be a constraint to investment. Too early to say what if anything we might want to propose on this front, but we can’t not have the debate given the imperative to be financially self-sustaining in a world of high inflation and possibly lower income trickling down from the sport’s Indian TV mothership.

For now, though, it’s diaries at the ready for the release of the 2027 fixture calendar later this month. Hope to see you in Hove in April and beyond!

Fight for the right to party

No doubt LA28 will be the brashest, noisiest Olympics and Paralympics yet. I’m intrigued in that context by a Sky News report that the US Olympic and Paralympic Committee has engaged advisors to try and sell a stake in Team USA’s commercial rights. 

Smart timing and a bold move if true – one which perhaps could only work in the massive American market. It may be too late for any fresh funds raised to boost medal prospects for 2028, but we should expect enormous US success on home soil regardless. And it might help Team USA put a lock on future medal tables. Over to you Team GB.

Seven nation army

If Andy Burnham wants a sense of the challenge in mounting a successful bid to host the 2040 Olympics and Paralympics in the north of England, he need only reflect on the list of seven nations that have formally expressed an interest in hosting the 2036 Games: Germany, Hungary, India, Qatar, South Africa, South Korea, Turkey.

The International Olympic Committee will conclude its choice of host in early 2029. Whichever countries get close but fall just short may well reload for 2040. My money remains on 2048 for Great Britain, 100 years on from the second London Olympics.

Ed Warner is chair of Sussex Cricket and GB Wheelchair Rugby and writes his sport column at sportinc.substack.com

    This comes as the cyber insurance market is already facing a turbulent time as a result of agentic AI hacks posing new challenges and threats. City AM reported in September that underwriters and insurers are considering limiting coverage until they can quantify the risk this tech poses and price it.

    Government proposals to scrap non-compete clauses may have ‘significant implications’ for the wider professional services sector.

    In the Budget, John Healey confirmed that the government is introducing legislation to reform non-compete clauses in employment contracts across the economy, in a bid to lubricate the labour marker for startups and scaling firms. The government will publish the details of the legislation early next year.

    Ministers have said it will focus on ‘workers’, meaning ‘equity partners’ are unlikely to be part of this overhaul. But for the professional services sector, “high-ranking senior associates and some salaried partners whose relationship with their firm will typically be governed by an employment contract” could be caught in the changes, explained Pooja Dasgupta, senior associate, Farrer & Co.

    The professional services sector relies heavily on senior individuals with strong client connections. Abigail Fisher, chief people officer at Grant Thornton UK, said: “The professional services sector is ultimately built on the strength of its people, relationships and expertise.”

    Non-competes increasinlgy common in consultancy

    Non-competes are clauses in an employment contract that legally restrict people from working for a direct rival or setting up a competing practice for a set period after leaving. Essentially they are used to prevent client relationships from walking out of the door of the firm.

    Firms in the professional services sector take these clauses seriously. City AM understands that the Big Four firms and other firms have tightened non-competes in recent years, with some clauses reportedly running for up to two years.

    James Ransome, partner at Patrick Morgan, said: “If those restrictions are removed or reduced, I would expect greater movement between firms.” Ransome added that it could have “significant implications” for the Big Four giants, as challenger consultancies could benefit from moving over senior talent.

    Some firms have started to dilute equity pools to protect partner profits during the sector slowdown, including KPMG, which demoted senior equity partners in April and swapped them into salaried partner roles.

    However, this side of the industry differs from the legal sector, as Nick Woolf, partner at Woolf&Co, explained: “most [legal] partners are LLP members, whose restrictions are typically contained in partnership agreements”, and therefore these clauses don’t have any effect.

    Gardening leave to the rescue

    Despite this proposal, City lawyers have already been 10 steps ahead with alternatives, including firms leaning more on gardening leave instead. Gardening leave is a contract clause that outlines the period when an employee stays on the payroll during their notice period after resigning or being dismissed, but is instructed to stay away from the workplace and not perform any duties.

    Ransome added that “deferred cash compensation, unit allocations, profit-sharing arrangements and other financial incentives can be equally powerful in retaining talent”. He added that “for partners who are several years into their tenure, the prospect of walking away from significant unvested financial benefits can be a greater deterrent than the non-compete itself.”
