]]> Maxwell Aircraft has unveiled plans for a new amphibious aircraft that combines a proven flying-boat design with modern composite construction and twin electric propulsion.

Designed to deliver capable performance both on the water and in the air, Maxwell Aircraft states that its M1 “builds on decades of development and experience, bringing together traditional seaplane characteristics with the potential benefits of electric flight.”

With its combination of manoeuvrability, useful payload and carefully considered water-handling features, the M1 has been designed to offer a practical and modern approach to amphibious aircraft operation, adds the company.

A proven design with a long aviation heritage

The M1’s origins can be traced through several generations of flying-boat development, beginning with the Grumman Widgeon.

Originally designed for the civil market, the Widgeon was produced between 1941 and 1955 and also served as a small patrol and utility aircraft with the US Navy during the Second World War.

Following the war, Grumman refined the design for civilian use, introducing improvements to the hull and increasing the cabin capacity to six seats.

The aircraft subsequently evolved into the Super Widgeon, with further improvements to its hull, windows, engines and propellers introduced by McKinnon in 1958.

Although relatively few examples were produced, the Widgeon established a foundation for future amphibious aircraft development.

Also read: Australia’s Albatross 2.0 could revitalise the golden age of flying boats Also read: Australia’s Albatross 2.0 could revitalise the golden age of flying boats

From the Gweduck to the M1

The next significant chapter began in 1990, when seaplane pilots Ben Ellison and Ross Mahon recognised the potential for a modern interpretation of the classic flying boat.

Inspired by the Widgeon, they set out to develop an aircraft combining traditional amphibious capabilities with contemporary aerodynamic and structural design.

Working alongside aircraft designer Marty Ellison, the team developed the concept for what would become the Gweduck. Its design prioritised water handling, with particular attention paid to take-off, landing and manoeuvrability in busy marine environments.

Features such as reversible propellers, a retractable water rudder and individually retractable wingtip floats were incorporated to make operating and mooring the aircraft easier. The hull was also carefully developed to improve pitch stability and minimise spray reaching the propellers.

The Gweduck first flew in 2009, demonstrating the success of the development programme and establishing a proven platform for subsequent development.

Modern composite construction and electric propulsion

A further development came with the introduction of carbon fibre and Kevlar construction. Walter Fellows recognised the potential to improve the Gweduck’s structural characteristics through the use of stronger, lighter and stiffer composite materials.

The acquisition of Composite Creations in Prineville, Oregon, provided the foundation for serial production of the aircraft in the experimental category. This marked an important step in the evolution of the design and established the basis for the next generation of development.

The M1 takes this established airframe concept in a new direction through electric propulsion. Its configuration features twin 400-horsepower electric motors, with Maxwell Aircraft highlighting weight savings of more than 1,100 lbs compared with the previous configuration.

The aircraft also benefits from an all-carbon-fibre and Kevlar construction, designed to provide strength and durability while eliminating the corrosion concerns associated with conventional metallic structures.

Designed for performance on water and in the air

In a press release, Maxwell Aircraft said that water handling remains central to the M1’s design philosophy.

Its flying-boat configuration is intended to provide superior performance in rough-water conditions, while the high-wing layout and retractable floats contribute to practical operation around docks and other waterfront facilities.

The twin motors feature instantly reversible propellers, providing precise control when manoeuvring on the water and assisting with docking.

The aircraft’s main landing gear tyres also protrude slightly to act as protective bumpers alongside docks, helping to reduce the risk of damage during mooring.

These practical details reflect the original Gweduck philosophy in that an amphibious aircraft should be designed not simply to fly efficiently, but also to operate safely and conveniently in its marine environment.

M1 performance and specifications

Maxwell Aircraft quotes a cruise speed of 135 knots and a total range of 205 miles. Its stated useful range is 170 miles, allowing for a 35-mile reserve to support safety and battery-life preservation.

The aircraft also offers a useful payload of 544 kg (1,200 lbs), providing considerable carrying capability for its intended role.

Combined with its twin electric motors and lightweight composite airframe, these figures position the M1 as an interesting development in the amphibious aircraft market.

Its design brings together the practical advantages of a flying boat with the performance characteristics of modern electric propulsion.

An evolution of amphibious aviation

The M1 is the latest stage in a development story spanning more than three decades, building on the experience gained from the Widgeon and Gweduck programmes.

Rather than starting from a completely new airframe concept, Maxwell Aircraft has taken an established amphibious design philosophy and adapted it for a new era of aviation.

By combining composite construction, electric power and features specifically developed for water-based operation, the M1 aims to demonstrate how traditional flying-boat capabilities can evolve to meet modern requirements.

With its emphasis on practical handling, useful payload and electric propulsion, the M1 offers an intriguing vision for the future of amphibious flight.

]]> Pakistan has successfully flight-tested its indigenously developed Fa’az air-to-air missile from a JF-17 Thunder fighter, marking a step towards equipping the country’s combat aircraft with locally developed weapons.

The Pakistan Air Force’s Directorate General of Public Relations (PAF DGPR) announced the test on 3 November, releasing footage of a JF-17 launching the missile from an underwing pylon.

“Pakistan has conducted successful flight test of first indigenously developed Fa’az air-to-air missile,” the PAF DGPR said in a statement on X.

“Fa’az will significantly enhance operational flexibility of Pakistan Air Force, further strengthening the country’s overall defense posture.”

The air force said the missile would improve its operational flexibility and strengthen Pakistan’s defence capabilities.

The footage shows a JF-17 Block I fighter, serial number 09-109, firing the Fa’az-IIR, the imaging infrared-guided version of the missile.

Pakistan has not disclosed the test location, launch range, target details or whether the missile successfully intercepted an aerial target.

What is the JF-17 Thunder?

The JF-17 is a single-engine, multirole combat aircraft jointly developed by Pakistan Aeronautical Complex (PAC) and China’s Chengdu Aircraft Corporation.

Designed as a relatively affordable fighter, it can undertake air defence, ground attack and reconnaissance missions. The aircraft is central to Pakistan’s efforts to maintain a combat fleet while developing its domestic aerospace industry.

The JF-17 has entered service in several versions, with the newer Block III incorporating more advanced avionics, including an active electronically scanned array radar.

The aircraft used in the Fa’az test was an earlier Block I model.

According to Pakistani defence publication Quwa, the aircraft was among the first JF-17s to undergo a major overhaul at PAC, beginning in 2019.
Pakistan already operates Chinese air-to-air missiles on its JF-17 fleet. These include the SD-10, an export version of China’s PL-12 radar-guided missile, while the newer Block III can carry the longer-range PL-15E.

The Fa’az programme is intended to give Pakistan a domestic alternative and greater control over the development and supply of weapons for its fighters.

What is the Fa’az missile?

Fa’az is a beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile developed by Pakistan’s Air Weapons Complex, part of the National Engineering and Scientific Commission (NESCOM).

It is marketed by the state-owned Global Industrial and Defence Solutions (GIDS), which publicly displayed the missile at the IDEF defence exhibition in Turkiye in July 2023.

The Fa’az-1 family has two guidance options.

The Fa’az-IIR, used in the latest test, relies on an imaging infrared seeker to identify and track the heat signature of an aircraft.

Unlike a conventional heat-seeking missile that tracks a strong infrared source, an imaging seeker produces a thermal image of the target. This can help distinguish an aircraft from background heat and countermeasures.

The second version, Fa’az-RF, uses an active radar seeker, allowing the missile to detect and track a target using its own radar during the final stage of flight.

Both versions are intended for engagements beyond the pilot’s visual range.

According to specifications published by Air Weapons Complex and detailed by Quwa, the Fa’az-IIR has an advertised range exceeding 75 kilometres and a maximum speed above Mach 3.2.

The radar-guided Fa’az-RF is advertised by the company with a range exceeding 100 kilometres and a speed above Mach 3.5.

The missile is approximately 3.95 metres long, weighs about 205 kilograms and uses a dual-thrust rocket motor.

Its guidance system is designed to receive targeting updates during flight before the seeker takes over for the final approach.

Why the test matters

Pakistan’s missile development comes as the PAF continues to rely heavily on imported weapons, particularly from China and the United States.

Its J-10C and JF-17 Block III fighters can carry the Chinese PL-15E beyond-visual-range missile, while its F-16 fleet uses the American AIM-120 AMRAAM.

Defence publication The War Zone (TWZ) reported that the Fa’az design has similarities to China’s SD-10/PL-12 missile family. However, GIDS maintains that the missile was developed locally and that it owns the associated intellectual property.

TWZ also quoted Douglas Barrie, senior fellow for military aerospace at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, who raised the possibility that the missile’s seeker technology could have Chinese origins. That remains unconfirmed.

The November test demonstrates that the Fa’az-IIR has progressed beyond the mockups displayed in 2023 to an airborne launch from a frontline fighter.

It does not yet establish when the missile will enter operational service.

Pakistan has also disclosed plans for an improved Fa’az-2 missile, advertised with a range of 180 kilometres, although no flight-test schedule has been announced.

]]> AerFin acquires 44 Boeing 737-800s from Qantas in landmark deal https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/aerfin-acquires-44-boeing-737ng-qantas/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 12:21:10 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55767 The deal marks a significant milestone in AerFin's expansion strategy, strengthening its position in the global aviation aftermarket.

The post AerFin acquires 44 Boeing 737-800s from Qantas in landmark deal appeared first on AGN.

]]> British aviation aftermarket specialist AerFin has agreed to acquire 44 Boeing 737 Next Generation (NG) aircraft from Australian flag carrier Qantas in what represents the largest transaction in the company’s history.

Announced on 4 November, the agreement covers 44 Boeing 737-800 aircraft and their 88 CFM International CFM56-7B engines. The deal marks a significant milestone in AerFin’s expansion strategy, strengthening its position in the global aviation aftermarket while supporting Qantas’ ongoing fleet renewal programme.

The aircraft will transfer to AerFin over the next seven years, with the first deliveries expected before the end of 2026. The phased arrangement will allow Qantas to continue operating its existing Boeing 737 fleet while progressively introducing newer-generation aircraft, such as the A321neo.

For AerFin, the acquisition provides a substantial portfolio of aircraft and engine assets to support airlines, maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) organisations, lessors and other aviation customers worldwide.

Largest acquisition in AerFin’s history

The transaction represents a major step forward for AerFin, which specialises in acquiring, managing, trading, leasing and disassembling commercial aircraft and engines, alongside supplying aircraft components.

The company intends to use the newly acquired assets to strengthen its global aftermarket offering, providing customers with access to used serviceable material (USM), engine components and other aviation parts.

AerFin Chief Executive Officer Simon Goodson described the transaction as a defining moment in the company’s development, highlighting its scale as evidence of AerFin’s ambition, technical expertise and financial capability.

Founded in 2010, AerFin has developed a substantial international presence, supporting more than 600 customers across six continents. Its activities include aircraft and engine trading, leasing, component sales, repair management and engine maintenance solutions.

The Qantas agreement further demonstrates the company’s ability to secure large-scale aircraft transactions and extract value from assets throughout their operational and aftermarket lifecycles.

Qantas accelerates Boeing 737 fleet renewal

For Qantas, the agreement forms part of a wider strategy to modernise its fleet and progressively transition away from its established Boeing 737-800 aircraft.

The Boeing 737 has been central to Qantas’ domestic operations for many years, serving routes across Australia’s extensive domestic network and selected short-haul international destinations.

According to Planespotters.net, the carrier still operates 76 Boeing 737-9800s with an average age of 18 years.

However, the airline is increasingly introducing newer-generation Airbus aircraft to improve operational efficiency, passenger experience and fleet economics.

Its renewal programme includes the Airbus A321XLR, which will gradually assume a greater role in domestic and regional operations. Qantas originally ordered 28 A321XLR aircraft in 2022 before adding another 20 to its commitment.

The airline has indicated that it expects to receive up to 24 new aircraft during 2026, supporting its wider fleet modernisation ambitions.

Qantas Domestic Chief Executive Markus Svensson said the Boeing 737s would continue to play an important role in the airline’s operations for several years, alongside its expanding next-generation fleet.

The agreement with AerFin will allow Qantas to plan the retirement of most of its Boeing 737 aircraft while retaining flexibility over the timing of individual departures as replacement aircraft arrive.

This flexibility is particularly important when replacing a large narrowbody fleet without disrupting capacity or operational reliability.

Significant opportunities in the aviation aftermarket

The acquisition also highlights the growing importance of the aviation aftermarket as airlines modernise their fleets. Aircraft retirement does not necessarily signal the end of an asset’s commercial usefulness.

Engines, landing gear, avionics, auxiliary power units and numerous other components can retain considerable value after an aircraft completes its airline service.

Through its acquisition of 44 aircraft and 88 engines, AerFin will gain access to a substantial volume of material that can be redistributed across the global aviation supply chain.

The CFM56-7B engine is particularly significant. Manufactured by CFM International, a joint venture between GE Aerospace and Safran Aircraft Engines, it powers the Boeing 737 Next Generation family and is one of the most widely operated commercial turbofan engines.

Its extensive global installed base creates an established market for replacement components, repair services and maintenance material.

As airlines seek to control maintenance expenditure and manage supply-chain challenges, demand for certified used serviceable components remains an important part of the aftermarket.

AerFin’s acquisition therefore provides an opportunity to expand its inventory and strengthen its ability to supply airlines and MRO providers with parts for ongoing maintenance requirements.

Strengthening AerFin’s international position

The Qantas agreement comes amid continued growth in the aircraft asset management and aftermarket sector. With airlines balancing fleet replacement programmes against rising maintenance costs and supply-chain pressures, specialist companies capable of acquiring, managing and redistributing aircraft assets are becoming increasingly important.

AerFin’s business model focuses on extracting value from aircraft and engines through trading, leasing, component management and maintenance support.

The transaction is particularly notable because of its scale and the inclusion of both complete aircraft and their associated engines. It also strengthens AerFin’s position in the Asia-Pacific region, an important growth market for the business.

The deal coincides with another significant development in AerFin’s ownership structure. Aviation Week reported that Japanese-backed ORIX Aviation completed its acquisition of AerFin on 2 November, making the company a wholly owned subsidiary.

This change provides important context for AerFin’s development as it continues to expand its asset portfolio and international market presence. The combination of new ownership and the largest acquisition in the company’s history signals a potentially significant period of growth.

For AerFin, the agreement creates a long-term pipeline of aircraft and engine assets that can support its aftermarket operations for years to come.

Ultimately, the transaction represents a significant development for both companies. Qantas gains greater flexibility as it modernises its fleet, while AerFin secures a major portfolio of established Boeing 737NG aircraft and CFM56-7B engines.

As the aviation industry continues to navigate fleet renewal, maintenance demand and supply-chain pressures, the agreement demonstrates the important role specialist aftermarket companies play in extending the commercial value of aircraft beyond their original airline service.

]]> Saudia unveils new premium economy cabin with 43” seat pitch on Boeing 787s from 2027 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/saudia-premium-economy-cabin-seats-2027/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 11:11:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55718 Unveiled at WTM London 2026, Saudia's new premium economy combines 43-inch seat pitch with a planned rollout across its long-haul fleet.

The post Saudia unveils new premium economy cabin with 43” seat pitch on Boeing 787s from 2027 appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • Saudia is entering premium economy with one of the roomiest products in the market, offering up to 43 inches of seat pitch.
  • The new Boeing 787 premium economy cabin pairs 43-inch pitch with 15.5-inch screens and enhanced privacy features.
  • Saudia plans to expand premium economy beyond new 787s, retrofitting selected A330, 777 and existing Dreamliner aircraft.

Saudia has unveiled its first premium economy cabin at World Travel Market (WTM) London 2026, confirming plans to introduce the new seats on Boeing 787 Dreamliners arriving next year.

The Saudi Arabian flag carrier presented the product on 3 November as part of its wider fleet modernisation and cabin refurbishment programme, known as the New Saudia Experience.

The new seats will offer up to 43” pitch, a 15.5” inflight entertainment screen, an extendable calf rest, additional personal storage and enhanced privacy.

Saudia also plans to retrofit selected Airbus A330, Boeing 777 and existing Boeing 787 aircraft, extending the product across its long-haul fleet.

What passengers can expect from Saudia’s premium economy seats

The new Saudia premium economy cabin will sit between economy and business class, offering passengers more space and comfort without the cost of a fully flat business-class seat.

With up to 43” pitch, Saudia’s premium economy product will offer considerably more legroom than conventional economy seating.

It also exceeds the seat pitch offered by several established premium economy products. Emirates, for example, offers up to 40” pitch in its premium economy cabin.

The 15.5” entertainment screen and extendable calf rest will improve entertainment and comfort on longer flights. In-seat storage provides more room for personal belongings.

Aviation Business News identifies Safran as the seat manufacturer, although Saudia’s announcement does not specify the supplier or seat model.

Executive Traveller reports that the new Boeing 787 cabin will include 21 premium economy seats arranged in three rows in a 2-3-2 configuration.

Saudia premium economy: Key facts

  • 43-inch seat pitch
  • 15.5-inch entertainment screen
  • Launches in 2027
  • Debuts on Boeing 787 Dreamliners
  • 21 seats in a 2-3-2 layout
  • Retrofits planned for selected A330s, 777s and existing 787s
  • Part of the New Saudia Experience programme

Saudia expands its premium cabin offering.

In the airline’s announcement, Arved von zur Muehlen, Saudia’s chief commercial officer, said of the new cabin: 

“The introduction of Premium Economy marks another step in enhancing the choices and comfort available to our guests. As part of the ‘New Saudia Experience’, we continue to invest in our onboard products and services to deliver a more comfortable and seamless journey.”

The airline is investing in new Boeing 787 aircraft while also introducing longer-range narrowbody services with the Airbus A321XLR.

Saudia also used World Travel Market to showcase the A321XLR’s business-class cabin, featuring 24 fully flat suites with direct aisle access and 120 economy seats.

The aircraft joined Saudia’s fleet earlier this year, making it the first airline in the Middle East and Africa to operate the A321XLR.

The carrier previously detailed its A321XLR cabin plans, including its choice of Thompson Aero Seating’s VantageSOLO business-class suites.

Saudia has also updated amenity kits and dining serviceware as part of its onboard hospitality offering.

#MoreToFlyFor Imbued with Saudi hospitality in every fine detail 💫✈️💚 Redefining your travel experience with an all-new collection of onboard essentials, crafted exclusively for First, Business, and Guest Classes 👝🍽️🎧✨ #ThisIsHowWefly https://t.co/ZGpxSQkge0

— Saudia (@SaudiAirlinesEn) June 1, 2026

The introduction of premium economy brings Saudia into the growing mix of international airlines that have introduced the “happy middle” cabin, first developed by EVA Air and Virgin Atlantic more than three decades ago.

While many airlines were slow to adopt the cabin, increased demand for premium cabin experiences following COVID-19 has encouraged airlines to expand cabin options for passengers seeking more comfort than standard economy.

]]> NASA unveils X-70 Fractal experimental aircraft to test advanced flight controls https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/nasa-x-70-fractal-experimental-aircraft/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:15:24 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55729 NASA has revealed the X-70 Fractal, a new crewed research aircraft capable of cruising at Mach 0.75 and reaching 45,000 feet to test advanced flight-control technology.

The post NASA unveils X-70 Fractal experimental aircraft to test advanced flight controls appeared first on AGN.

]]> NASA has unveiled the X-70 Fractal, a new crewed experimental aircraft designed to test advanced flight-control systems and explore new levels of aircraft manoeuvrability. The agency expects the aircraft to make its first flight under NASA operations within two years.

NASA announced the new X-plane on 4 November during the UP.Summit at NASA’s Kennedy Space Centre in Florida.

The X-70 Fractal will be a flexible research platform, allowing engineers to test emerging aviation technologies in flight rather than relying solely on simulations or ground-based experiments.

Its rapidly reconfigurable flight-control system would support manoeuvres that NASA says have never previously been demonstrated in crewed flight.

“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, manoeuvrability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

What are the X-70 Fractal’s capabilities?

The X-70 is designed to cruise at Mach 0.75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet and operate over distances of approximately 1,500 nautical miles (2,778 km). Its maximum takeoff weight is 10,000 lb (4,536 kg).

X-70 Specifications
Specification X-70 Fractal
Aircraft type Crewed experimental aircraft
Cruise speed Mach 0.75
Maximum altitude 45,000 ft
Operational range Approx. 1,500 nautical miles
Takeoff weight 10,000 lb
Experimental payload capacity Up to 2,000 lb

The aircraft will accommodate up to 2,000 lb (907 kg) of experimental equipment, carried internally or externally.

“Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next,” Isaacman said.

X-70 joins NASA’s X-59 and historic experimental aircraft

The X-70 is the latest addition to NASA’s long-running experimental aircraft programme, which has contributed to advances in high-speed flight, aerodynamics and aircraft technology.

Previous X-planes include the Bell X-1, which became the first crewed aircraft to exceed the speed of sound in level flight in 1947, and the rocket-powered X-15, which conducted hypersonic research during the 1950s and 1960s.

NASA is also continuing work on the X-59 quiet supersonic aircraft, designed to reduce the sonic boom and collect data on the sound generated by supersonic flight.

The X-70 will investigate advanced flight-control systems and manoeuvrability.

“For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” said Laurie Grindle, director of the Aeronautics Division within NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”

Why is NASA developing another X-plane?

The X-70 will expand NASA’s capacity to conduct flight research, particularly in advanced flight controls and aircraft handling.

Unlike experimental aircraft developed around a single technology, the Fractal will accommodate different research equipment and flight-test objectives. Its reconfigurable controls could allow researchers to investigate how new control systems affect aircraft behaviour across a range of flight conditions. 

“We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics,” Isaacman said. “This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.”

 the chat header), and "height:auto" overrode that sizing and let them
 balloon to full intrinsic size. The real, measured CLS cause is the font
 swap handled above; any genuinely-unsized content image should get
 width/height attributes on the tag itself, not a blanket src selector. */
 /* Homepage auto-playing chat demo: the typing animation appends message
 bubbles and result cards, which used to GROW the demo window and push
 everything below it on every cycle (measured: CLS 0.258 on the
 homepage). Fixed internal heights make the animation play inside a
 constant-size box — newest messages stick to the bottom like a real
 chat, the results tray keeps its space reserved. */
 #lh-demo-chat {

 justify-content: flex-end;
 overflow: hidden;
 }

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.

 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {

 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {

 justify-content: flex-end;

 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__RECTORS_Q1.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The implementation of the strategic plan is monitored</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>International activity, including co-operation projects and mobility should be carefully monitored. Clear and unambiguous monitoring of such activity are key to ensuring success. Explicit indicators should be developed to show specific success scenarios. The indicators should be SMART.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support measures are provided to staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants. For example:  allocation of additional resources, training on intercultural competences and other relevant aspects of the mob</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should allocate additional resources to support staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants, such as allowing staff adequate time to carry out work with outgoing and incoming participants and providing administrative back-up (e.g. with financial management). Trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, management of mobility projects’, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/the-effective-management-and-ownership-of-erasmus-for-internationalisation" target="_blank">The effective management and ownership of Erasmus +’ for ‘internationalisation’</a></div>

                            <div class="eche-report-officer-number-text">2</div>
                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q2.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for Erasmus+ mobility</div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on shared quality requirements, student and staff selection for mobility and clear timelines at all stages of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>A key role of Inter-Institutional Agreements is to set out agreed, shared quality criteria and clear timelines for all stages of the mobility.<br>Shared quality criteria may include, but are not limited to: selection criteria for the nomination of students and staff, recommended language skills, grading systems, measures for preparing, receiving and integrating Erasmus+ participants. These might be expanded with geographic and subject-specific criteria.<br>In terms of the timelines set out for the mobility activities, particular attention should be paid to:</p><ul><li>The nomination of mobile students by the sending HEI,</li><li>The acceptance of nominees, and</li><li>The issuing of the Transcript of Records after the study period abroad by the receiving HEI. This is normally issued within five weeks after the end date of the mobility period.</li></ul>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are regularly monitored and if necessary adapted.</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Establishing Inter-Institutional Agreements is only the first step in promoting mobility. Once signed, Agreements should be actively honoured and adjusted over time as needed. To ensure that an institution’s Inter-Institutional Agreements continue addressing well-defined needs and opportunities, such agreements should be monitored regularly both in quantitative (e.g. number of mobilities) and qualitative (e.g. shared quality criteria) terms. This can be done in a number of ways for example by a designated responsible individual, office or an established process. Seeking input from across the organisation helps create acceptance at all levels of the institution and reinforces commitment towards mobility.</p>                      </div>

                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The formal procedures for recognising student mobility should clearly and unambiguously set out the responsibilities of an appointed academic, who has the authority, on behalf of the appropriate academic body, to:</p><ul><li>Approve the Learning Agreements,</li><li>Exceptionally amend the Learning Agreements, and</li><li>Recognise the successfully completed activities, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams.</li></ul>                      </div>

                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>To ensure effective staff mobility, it has to be based on a signed mobility agreement. The mobility agreement has to acceptable and signed by all parties in advance. There are four key elements set out by the mobility agreement, which are intended to increase the relevance and potential impact of the mobility. These are:</p><ul><li>The overall objectives and academic rationale of the mobility,</li><li>The institutional requirements or strategy, and the mobility's added value in the context of modernisation and internationalisation,</li><li>The activities or teaching programme content to be undertaken by the staff member, and,</li><li>The expected outcomes and impact of the mobility on the professional development of the staff member at both institutions.</li></ul><p>For this to work effectively, there needs to be dialogue and discussion between the three parties prior to the signing of the mobility agreement having agreed the common goals which are acceptable.&nbsp;</p>                      </div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> During the mobility, your institution fosters the integration of the incoming mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>

                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution appoints responsible person(s) to deal with practical issues (e.g. social, health, and/or psychological problems)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should ensure there are named, visible persons who are responsible for the practical issues associated with integrating mobile students. This visibility should be ensured through introduction to this function during the Welcome / Orientation period and be detailed on the website so all mobile students can easily access this support, throughout their stay.&nbsp;</p><p>Non-academic mentoring and support arrangements should already be outlined in the Course Catalogue of the receiving HEI, in the section on general information for students, with relevant contact persons in the respective areas. Academic advisors should have close contact with the practical services which are available to incoming participants as they are often the first line of contact to the incoming student. Further information sessions should be arranged for all staff who work with incoming students to ensure they are adequately signposted on to the appropriate services they require.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It appoints responsible person(s) to deal with academic issues (course timetables, student attendance, coursework, relationship with academic staff, etc.)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is important that the receiving institution appoints specific named academic advisors who are responsible for dealing with problems related to academic issues (course timetables, student attendance, coursework, relationship with academic staff, etc.) of incoming students.&nbsp; Information on mentoring for thesis writing for incoming students is particularly important and clear mentoring arrangements should be agreed upon between the student, sending and receiving institutions and organised before the mobility.</p><p>For traineeships, a mentor, different from the supervisor, should be nominated to support and encourage the mobile student while in the receiving organisation. The mentor should also provide information on the culture of the enterprise and informal codes and conducts, of the receiving organisation. The contact details of both the supervisor and the mentor should be specified in the Learning Agreement.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It organises activities to integrate them in the receiving institution and the local community, e.g. with the support of student organisations, Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association etc.</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>As well as academic and practical support from the institution, incoming students need to feel fully integrated into the student community, something which is best done by their fellow students / peers. Local student association(s), such as Erasmus Student Network (ESN) and the other associations’ member of the ESAA - Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association (<a href="http://esaa-eu.org/">http://esaa-eu.org/</a>), play an important role in supporting incoming students. Incoming students need to feel welcomed and included in the student organisations. To help this process, the student organisations need to be aware of their role in supporting this integration and have access to the right resources, information, guidance and incentives. As institutions often have many types of student organisations, cooperation between them is encouraged through meetings together, social activities and buddy programmes. A key aspect of these activities is to make sure they are for all students so incoming students are integrated with the local students and hence the culture. Student organisations include for example, ESN (Erasmus Student Network) or ESAA - Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association (<a href="http://esaa-eu.org/">http://esaa-eu.org/</a>). ESAA runs a buddy system to encourage integration of incoming students with their peers inside the institution and share good practice with other member associations around Europe.</p>                      </div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> At the end of the mobility, your institution has formal procedures for recognising student mobility (good practices linked to recognition at the end of the mobility, e.g. in the use of Transcripts of Records and Grade Distribution Tables)</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records are issued in a timely manner (normally 5 weeks) to both incoming and outgoing students</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is highly important in the recognition framework to provide Transcripts of Records in a timely manner, immediately following the mobility period. After the mobility, the receiving institution should send a Transcript of Records to the student and to the sending institution within a period stipulated in the Inter-Institutional Agreement (normally within five weeks after publication/proclamation of the student’s results at the receiving institution). It can be provided electronically or through any other means accessible to the student and the sending institution. The Transcript of Records from the receiving institution should refer to the educational components agreed upon in the Learning Agreement. Grade distribution information should be included as well, either as a web link or an annex.</p><p>Following the receipt of the Transcript of Records from the receiving institution, the sending institution should automatically transfer and recognise the student’s academic outcomes successfully completed at the receiving institution, as agreed in the Learning Agreement, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. The Sending Institution will provide a Transcript of Records to the student or record the results in a database or any other means accessible to the student, normally within five weeks after having received the transcript of the receiving institution. The EU official template for the Learning Agreement for studies (including the Transcript of Records) is available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records of incoming students include, where applicable, a Grade Distribution Table for the programme of study, according to the ECTS Users’ Guide</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Where applicable, the Sending Institution should translate the grades received by the student abroad. To enable the Sending Institution to do so, it is highly important for the receiving institution to provide a clear explanation of the institutional grading system and grade distribution in the department or study programme together with the Transcript of Records. Such information can be provided either through a web link or as an annex to the Transcripts of Records. Where applicable, use should be made of a Grade Distribution Table for the programme of study, according to the ECTS Users’ Guide (<a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm</a>).</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All credits gained by students during a period of study abroad that were specified in the final version of the Learning Agreement are automatically transferred by your institution and count towards the students' final degree, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The sending institution should ensure that all the credits earned by the mobile student during the mobility period are recognised and counted towards the final degree, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. The period of study abroad must be clear in the student's records and documents issued to the student (Diploma Supplement or equivalent). This is a golden rule of recognition of credit mobility within the framework of inter-institutional agreements. All the credits towards the student's degree that are earned during the mobility period and which were originally agreed on in the Learning Agreement (or a revised version to it) should be recognised by the sending HEI without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. Learning Agreements are binding for all the parties and require that, on successful completion of the mobility period, the sending HEI recognises credits earned by the student and documents these credits in the student records, so they can be identified in a transparent way.</p><p>Upon receipt of the Transcript of Records or Training Certificates, the sending HEI should:<br>a) certify the mobile student has fulfilled all requirements stipulated in the Learning Agreement;<br>b) ensure recognition of the mobility period abroad within the time-scale and according to the conditions stipulated in the institutional recognition framework.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records of incoming students include a description of or a link to the national grading system</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The Transcript of Records from the receiving institution should include grade distribution information, either as a web link or an annex. The local grading scale should be clearly explained, with a statistical distribution of local grades, to provide transparency and understanding of grading practices at the host institution. Where applicable, use should be made of a Grade Distribution Table for the programme of study, according to the ECTS Users’ Guide (<a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm</a>).</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records of outgoing students provide details of the courses taken abroad</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The Transcript of Records should ensure a transparent recognition of the study period abroad, providing details of the courses the students undertook while studying abroad, including:</p><ul><li>Component code (if any)</li><li>Component title at the Receiving Institution&nbsp; (as indicated in the course catalogue)</li><li>If the component was successfully completed by the student?</li><li>Number of ECTS credits (or equivalent)</li><li>Grades received at the Receiving Institution</li></ul><p>The EU official template for the Learning Agreement (including the Transcript of Records) is available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;</a>&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Grades of outgoing students are converted, if applicable, according to a fair and transparent methodology communicated before the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Grades of outgoing students are converted, if applicable, according to a fair and transparent methodology communicated before the mobility. There are more details on this in the ECTS Users’ Guide.</p>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">To all students, automatically, free of charge and in a major European language</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>This Supplement should include a record of the period of mobility under the Erasmus+ Programme. The 48 European countries taking part in the Bologna Process have agreed that each mobile graduate in their respective country should receive the Diploma Supplement (DS) automatically, free of charge and in at least one of the major European languages in addition to the national language. The HEI should issue a Diploma Supplement (or equivalent) to accompany every degree successfully completed by a student, using - where applicable - the template developed by the European Commission, the Council of Europe and UNESCO. The HEI's policy on issuing the Diploma Supplement should be published on its website.</p><p>The template for the Diploma Supplement is available at:<br><a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/tools/diploma-supplement_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/tools/diploma-supplement_en.htm&nbsp;</a></p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">That includes a record of the mobility period(s) carried out by the student under the Erasmus+ programme</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The information contained in the Transcript of Records from the Receiving Institution should also be included in the Diploma Supplement produced by the Sending Institution (at least for Sending Institutions located in Programme Countries), with the exact titles of the components that the student has followed abroad. Alongside modules or units taken at the sending HEI, the Diploma Supplement should list recognised modules, units and/or training activities undertaken during the student's mobility period and indicate the location of these mobility activities.<br>In the case of double, multiple or joint degrees, the Diploma Supplement should indicate the name and status of the partner HEIs awarding the degree and explain the respective language(s) of instruction and examination. In addition, an explanation should be provided about the grading and classification scheme agreed by the awarding HEIs. The template for the Diploma Supplement is available at:<br><a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/tools/diploma-supplement_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/tools/diploma-supplement_en.htm</a>&nbsp;</p>                      </div>
